speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I move, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." I will refer to this Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill (RH Bill) as the RH Bill – short for racial harmony, which is somewhat similar sounding to the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, which we passed some time ago.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The latter amends the President's powers under the Constitution to give effect to the proposals in this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will, of course, take the Constitution Bill through its formal stages separately later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And at the same time, by presenting it in this form, we seek to affirm the importance of racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That, we try to deal with, try and improve conduct, try and get people together, through a variety of policies and platforms which promote social cohesion and racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law can set out a framework as to what you cannot do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can also access this material through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As long as Members understand we are consolidating from different pieces of legislation and so, when you express your concerns and so on, in a way, what you need to understand is, if you have those concerns, then they would have existed for a very long time, because this Bill does not create new provisions in a substantive manner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some new provisions – you can see that in the Bill and in the press releases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am referring to the substantive provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Table in Annex 1 also provides a comparative reference between this Bill and the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act as well as other legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Part 2 of the Bill on the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony takes reference from the current Presidential Council for Religious Harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part 3 of the Bill on "Restraining Orders Against Racial Content" and Part 4 of the Bill on "Measures Against Foreign Influence" are also similar to the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part 6 of the Bill on "Offences Relating to Race" – those are what I call the charging provisions – brings over the existing offences from the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the course of bringing in concepts and provisions from other existing legislation, we have made some refinements to some provisions for clarity and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that is a more fundamental, more important question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is because we have always treated racial harmony as being fundamental in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill has to be seen in that context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Multiracialism, underpinned by racial harmony, is a foundational principle for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proximate cause were the racial riots of 1964.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that time, communal tensions were very high in both Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was during a procession to celebrate the Prophet Muhammad's birthday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A glass bottle was thrown into a crowd.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was then an angry exchange between Malays in the crowd and some Chinese bystanders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That resulted in violence and the violence spread all across Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, riots broke out again on 2 September 1964, between again the Malays and Chinese.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That happened after a Malay trishaw rider was killed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The broader context for those tensions were the arguments between Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These arguments then led to Singapore's separation from Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore's merger into the new Federation of Malaysia in 1963 had raised some very fundamental issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Although the new state of Malaysia in 1963 had Malays, Chinese, Indians and Eurasians, amongst others, there were basic differences between Singapore and Kuala Lumpur on how the state was to be organised and, in particular, the approach towards multiracialism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The idea of a "Malaysian Malaysia", advocated by Singapore, brought about a very strong counter from the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) leaders in Kuala Lumpur and Malaya.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They saw this as a challenge to Malay dominance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the day of our Independence on 9 August 1965, Mr Lee said – and these are very important words.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He famously said, "We are going to have a multiracial nation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not a Malay nation; this is not a Chinese nation; this is not an Indian nation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everybody will have his place: equal, language, culture, religion." These issues and the approaches exercised the minds of Mr Lee and his generation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had grown up in a Malaya where different races had lived together for generations as colonial subjects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once Independence was achieved – first in the Federation of Malaya in 1957 and then in Malaysia in 1963 – the question immediately arose as to whether all citizens, regardless of their race, were to have equal status.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our founding leaders had seen how fragile a multiracial society could be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They wanted, as far as possible, to make Singapore a more racially equal society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some major Chinese organisations asked Mr Lee to make Chinese our only official language and the language of business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said on 3 October 1965 that, "although in Singapore 75% of the population is Chinese, the Malays form only 12%, never mind; Malay has become our national language, yet, Malay language, Chinese, Tamil and English are all equal." The four official languages were given recognition by the Republic of Singapore Independence Act and also in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another example: one of the first few constitutional amendments our first generation of leaders made was to create a Presidential Council for Minority Rights chaired by the Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were several other steps that were taken to focus on a Singaporean identity which would transcend race and religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was an act of tremendous courage on the part of those leaders to do all of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would have been far easier for them to have said, "Okay, in Singapore, Chinese will be the sole official language and the Chinese will have several other legally recognised privileges." If you see the situation in advanced, developed countries, if you go to Germany, you have to speak German by and large, if you go to France, you have to speak French.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go to the United Kingdom (UK), you generally have to speak English.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it would have been very natural for some to have said in Singapore, Chinese should be the language of business, language of commerce and language of government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We were ranked first out of over 130 countries and territories for this question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government also periodically conducts domestic surveys on racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I would say to Members is that what we have in Singapore is actually not the natural order of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Indeed, there is nothing natural about what we have in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We now have come to believe it to be natural.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But actually, it is not natural because human beings are wired to be tribal, based on identity, and that continues to be true in many places around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at many countries, they are organised on the basis of formal or informal racial or religious hierarchies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we have in Singapore is we changed the natural order and made that changed situation second nature for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this Bill has to be seen in that context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we consider our approach to multi-racialism and laws, it is also useful to look at the experience of other countries and see what we should do or should not do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UK, United States (US) and France have a majority white population, but also a long history of immigration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, they have been multiracial longer than Singapore has been independent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Race has been a flashpoint in these countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, the UK was hit with a wave of riots, between July and August 2024.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was a knife attack that killed three young girls.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rumours were that the attacker was an asylum seeker but, in fact, the attacker was born in the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By mid-afternoon on the day of the attack, the false name of the suspect had received more than 30,000 mentions on X alone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As of September last year, the police had arrested more than 1,200 persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This wave of riots is widely viewed as being among the most serious in British history.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It exposed deep-seated racist sentiments and also other grievances, relating to immigration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have also been other riots in the UK, arising from distrust between communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That survey was conducted by the King's College, University of Manchester and the University of Saint Andrews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The survey found that more than one-third of persons from minority groups in the UK had actually experienced racist assaults, meaning physical attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Turning to the US, we also see evidence that race and attitudes towards racial issues, seems to divide American society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see the endless media reports on the issue, the protests marches, the violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Reports of anti-semitic and anti-Muslim acts increased by almost 300% and 30% respectively, while other types of racist acts increased by around 20%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Racial tensions are present and spill into serious violence even in countries where people do not look very different from each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the 1994 Rwandan genocide, this is one of several examples in Africa.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A more recent example is the crisis in Sudan, specifically, the Darfur region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as a result of the crisis, millions have been displaced from their homes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The British Broadcasting Corporation recently described the situation in Sudan as the world's worst humanitarian crisis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In our region, too, many countries have faced serious and long-standing conflict along racial lines, Myanmar being one of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, looking across these countries, we see three issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of the countries I have cited as examples earlier, such as the US, UK and France, they allow denigration of other races or religions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US, the Supreme Court has said that inflammatory speech, even speech advocating violence, can be protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I told this House in my Ministerial Statement in April 2019, if we do not have a tough set of laws and policies against hateful and offensive speech, the tone and texture of public discourse in our society will change over time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will create an environment that is conducive for discrimination and eventually, violence against people who can be classified in a specific category, described by skin colour or religion or some other attribute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I trust that on this issue, we are all agreed as to where we draw the line on hate speech, on speech which advocates violence, on speech which incites violence, on speech which seeks to set aside a group and target them as the "out" group, as I have said in my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second lesson that I think that we can learn is and this is an age-old issue: the exploitation of race for politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Race-related issues have immense power to mobilise people, identity politics basically and it is deeply visceral.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Politicians know it, and many exploit it to score political points and win elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In recent years, you see a trend in many countries, including the West, politicians encouraging people to think along racial lines and adopt a "us versus them" mentality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if this is repeated both during electoral cycles and off-electoral cycles, the racial divisions are then reinforced and become even more entrenched in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I trust all Members will agree with us that the exploitation of race has no place in our politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The neighbours we have and our day-to-day interactions with them affect how we perceive the wider society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Racially segregated neighbourhoods limit opportunities to build trust between different communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a consequence of years of residential segregation based on race and the issue is not unique to the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the riots in 2001, the government in UK commissioned a study.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That study found that physical racial segregation of housing estates was a key contributor for the riots then.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The report described most of the white communities as living "parallel lives" from minority Asian and black groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It commented that, "there is little wonder that ignorance about each other's communities can easily grow into fear".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were to look at France, residential segregation can also be found in the banlieues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are suburban areas predominantly inhabited by immigrant families usually of Arab or other African descent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The overlap of ethnic segregation in these areas, with economic and social exclusion, has led to increasing polarisation between those minority, marginalised groups and the majority in French society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, here, we have done it differently in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Previous Governments had the foresight to introduce the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP) in our public housing estates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: EIP has ensured a mix of races in our public housing estates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Government had left it to market forces, you would have seen Chinese, Malays and Indians, forming residential enclaves in different parts of Singapore, similar to what is happening in many other countries and similar to what was happening in Singapore before we introduced the EIP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that happens, soon, schools in those areas would also become segregated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Children would have less diverse social circles and limited exposure to different cultures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They would grow up with less understanding, trust and comfort with other communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will carry this into adulthood and into workplaces.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We put in place rules to maintain certain racial proportions in public housing, so that we would have mixing across races in every estate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singaporeans generally appreciate the intent of this policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the light of these lessons, what is our approach to maintaining racial harmony?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, we have to have a strong legal framework which sets clear boundaries on what is not allowed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, with that framework in place, we would have to have the Government actively putting in place policies and platforms that maximise our common space, to strengthen cohesion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law can tell you what you cannot do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law cannot tell you "be nice to your neighbour, form friendships and bonds with your neighbours across races, across religions".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the thousands of activities that are carried out every weekend, bringing people together and multiplicity of events and approaches, the way schools are organised, every other aspect, which is too long to go into here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that comes in to create opportunities for people to become friends or at least form understandings and dislike each other less where there is dislike and like each other more where there is some potential for like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And over time, we would say that Singapore has progressed substantively on this front.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let me start with the first aspect: our a strong legal framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our Constitution guarantees that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection under the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is the responsibility of the Government to care for the interests of the racial minorities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minority representation in Parliament is guaranteed through our Group Representation Constituency (GRC) system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This means an employer cannot make an adverse employment decision because of the race of the jobseeker or employee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A subsequent Bill will lay out avenues for affected individuals to seek recourse when they feel that they have been discriminated against, including racial discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond that, of course, our Penal Code also sets out what conduct is not acceptable and that would include conduct in the context of race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These laws have generally served their intended purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill continues with that approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law tells us what is it that we cannot do or what remedies there are when something wrong has been done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second part: the policies and platforms to expand and deepen our common space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at 1965 and if you look at today, you will find that most people are comfortable with bonds across races.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is understanding, there is appreciation, there is acceptance and deep bonds across racial religious lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, there are some people who will still have some different viewpoints but, on the whole, it is a very substantively different society from what it was in the 1960s, because we have been facilitating interactions between people of different backgrounds and we do this very deliberately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While I do not want to go into a discussion of the policies, maybe I can refer to a poll.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is in the context where, in many parts of the world, race relations have actually regressed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is an increase of about 8% from 2018/2019, when 57.1% said that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of race-related incidents reported to the Police has also largely remained stable over the years at around 10 per year, though there are some years with spikes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police have noticed, I have noticed, that whenever there are elections, the number of Police reports spike.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we cannot take this state of affairs for granted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are in an age when identity politics is on the rise globally and we cannot cut ourselves off from the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that background, Sir, I will turn to the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, the Bill has five aspects or five proposals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That gives the offender the opportunity to mend ties with the community that he was attacking and we provide this as an alternative to the person being charged in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, the Bill seeks to establish a Restraining Order regime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fifth, it introduces safeguards against foreign influence through race-based entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 2024 poll on racial harmony, which I referred to, shows that the public strongly support various proposals in this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nonetheless, during public consultations, one common comment that we received was that this Bill only prevents racial disharmony and it does not promote racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What people want to see is something that will positively push people to be harmonious with each other across races.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained the point earlier: you cannot, by law, force people to get along better with each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is to come through government policies, through the framework, the structure of society and how we build that DNA into society over time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is what we have been doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Laws play an important role in that because if you allow bad behaviour, then these policies would not succeed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Laws are there, they provide a very strong legal framework and people know we will enforce our laws and, therefore, they reduce and deter bad behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once you stop that bad behaviour, amongst a small minority usually – laws are necessary, usually only as regards a small minority of people – then, if you do not allow for that behaviour, then there is a framework and within that, you can promote policies that will enhance racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will refer specifically to two proposals in this Bill, one relating to race-related offences and the other CRI.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleague, the Minister of State Sun Xueling, will cover the rest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are covered under clauses 39 and 40 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 39 takes what is already an offence today, that is, inciting violence under section 267C of the Penal Code and it prescribes increased penalties for a subset of that conduct where offenders do so on the basis of a belief about race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 40 brings over the substance of existing race-related offences in the Penal Code, which deal with threats to racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are: section 298, which concerns acts that wound the racial feelings of any person; and section 298A, which concerns acts that promote enmity between racial groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In bringing these offences over, we have made certain clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In particular, we have received public feedback that the term "wound racial feelings" lacks clarity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, clause 40(2) replaces the term "wound racial feelings" with objective descriptions, so, at least, more objective descriptions, which are, essentially, "insults, vilifies, denigrates, threatens or abuses on the basis of race".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This provides greater clarity and probably narrows the scope of conduct that would make out an offence today. "Wound racial feelings" could potentially be subjective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also aligned these offences with the corresponding offences in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act as we take an equally strong stance in dealing with threats to racial harmony and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the penalties for offences in this Bill are the same as the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we have also introduced defences for offences under clause 40 that are already present in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the defence of private or domestic conduct, which allows people to have a safe space to express their views about race and religion in private or domestic settings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The defence of pointing out, in good faith, any matters for the purpose of bringing about a removal of those matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And similar to the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, there will also be extraterritorial coverage for race-related offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the offence is committed overseas but targets Singapore and has an impact in Singapore, it will be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We acknowledge that it may be difficult to enforce offences outside of Singapore, but it signals our commitment to protect our racial harmony, even when the threat originates outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That said, while there are offences in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act that are tiered, depending on whether the act is committed by a religious leader or a lay person, this Bill makes no such differentiation for obvious reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law today does not distinguish between different categories of offenders for race-related offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The distinction we had drawn in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was unique because in the context of religion, it reflects a greater risk posed by the actions of religious leaders who exercise formal religious authority and there is no equivalent in the context of race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, all persons are held to the same standard since the acts of any individual can threaten racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, this only reflects the existing law and does not expand the scope of criminal liability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our starting point is this: racial incidents harm both the victim as well as the ties between the races.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is similar to the CRI in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and we seek to achieve two policy objectives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It provides the alleged offender with the opportunity to make amends for his racist conduct and hopefully, by that process, he or she gets a better understanding of the community that he attacked and hopefully, creates a bond, a bridge and strengthens mutual understanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It gives the offender the opportunity to learn from his mistake.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, raising awareness of how the alleged offender's racist conduct impacts others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, initiating action by requiring the alleged offender to make amends with the aggrieved individual and community through volunteer work and other suitable engagements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such cases will continue to be directly referred for prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By fostering an environment of trust, empathy and unity, we can build a future where everyone continues to feel a deep sense of belonging and pride in being Singaporean, regardless of race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is, in fact, very difficult and very hard work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But given that Singapore has always been a diverse country – many races, many religions, many languages – we had to and we wanted to, from this multiplicity, create one united people but without suppressing any racial, religious or linguistic identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has been, if I may say so, the genius of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We could not have done this without simultaneously fostering understanding, trust and acceptance amongst our many, and at the same time, making clear that we will not tolerate any bigotry or hatred or intolerance that threatens the one people that we have become.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are grateful for the progress we have made thanks to the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations of Singaporeans, but we know that we can do better and we are trying to do better.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill, as I have said earlier, will not be a panacea for solving all race-related challenges, but it is a powerful signal of our resolve to remain united as one people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us send a strong signal to all the nations of the world that 60 years after we gained Independence, Singapore will remain a multiracial nation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That we will not be a Malay nation, a Chinese nation, or an Indian nation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That every Singaporean will have his place here and that he or she will be respected, and we will all be equal: language, culture, race, religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling will now take the House through the remaining proposals in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: He also explained two of the five proposals on race-related offences and the Community Remedial Initiative (CRI).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will start with the Restraining Order regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This lever is not new in our statutes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act already has a Restraining Order regime against content that threatens religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This was deemed necessary because the Internet, social media and smartphones can enable offensive content to go viral very quickly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will complement existing levers, such as the Broadcasting Act and Online Criminal Harms Act, which provide ex-post powers against egregious race-related content on platforms, such as social media services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is one area where race is in a slightly different position as compared with religion, with regard to their respective roles in politics in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That difference is reflected in the difference between the Restraining Order regime under the Bill, and that in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have, as a society, emphasised that as a multi-religious but secular state, religion should not be mixed with politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is a foundational principle of our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the context of race, we have laws which deal with communal politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But given our multiracial community, race features in some of our political structures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We also have constitutional provisions to ensure that a President from a minority race will be elected periodically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Good faith discussions about race have always been an important part of our political discourse and will continue to be so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It would therefore not be right or possible to completely disallow racial discourse in politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Thus, this will not be one of the grounds for the issuance of a racial content Restraining Order in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, any behaviour that creates enmity between races, such as whipping up of communal feelings, denigration of a person’s race or encouragement of violence, have been and will continue to be prohibited by the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Restraining Order takes immediate effect once issued and this mirrors the amended Restraining Order process when the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was amended in 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is no need to first establish that the person is engaging in criminal conduct, as the intent is to quickly stop the spread of content that could potentially undermine social cohesion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Failure to comply with the Restraining Order will be an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government will be very careful when exercising its powers to issue Restraining Orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The fact that no Restraining Orders have been issued to date, since the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was introduced in 1990, is reflective of this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But neither is this an indication that the Restraining Order regime is not necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the contrary, the mere existence of the regime is a deterrent against conduct that disrupts religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The same logic applies to the Restraining Order regime under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The issuance of Restraining Orders will be subject to stringent safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: All Restraining Orders will be reviewed by a Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony, which I will elaborate on in the next proposal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The person who is issued a racial content Restraining Order will be able to make representations to the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony’s independent recommendation on the Restraining Order will thereafter be sent to the President, followed by the Cabinet’s advice to the President.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If the Cabinet’s advice is different from the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony’s recommendation, the President will be able to act in his discretion to confirm, cancel or vary the Restraining Order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony will comprise representatives from the major racial and religious communities in Singapore and those who have distinguished themselves in public service or community relations in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As with the existing Presidential Council for Religious Harmony, our intent is to ensure that the new Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony adequately represents the racial and religious diversity in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The proposal to replace the existing Presidential Council for Religious Harmony with the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony recognises that issues of race may have religious dimensions and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, having a single council would facilitate consultation by the Minister or Parliament on issues given the close relationship between race and religion in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To this end, the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony will have the following functions: one, to consider and report to the Minister or Parliament on matters affecting the maintenance of racial and religious harmony in Singapore which are referred to the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony by the Minister or by Parliament; and two, to consider and make recommendations to the President on Restraining Orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the context of this proposal, we will be introducing the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are the same powers that the President has today in relation to the Presidential Council for Religious Harmony and we are extending it to the new Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have consulted the President on these amendments as they pertain to his discretionary powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Moving to the last proposal, we want to safeguard our racial harmony from malicious foreign influence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our starting point is this: as a small, open and digitally inclusive society, Singapore is vulnerable to external actors exerting malicious foreign influence to achieve their own agenda.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We had thus introduced safeguards against malicious foreign influence for religious groups under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act in 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Similarly, entities that promote the interests of a racial group or discuss issues relating to race are potential entry points for malicious foreign influence, which may seek to exploit race for their own agenda and undermine our racial harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The same MDDI poll I mentioned earlier provided the following insights: one, nearly seven in 10 respondents agreed that Singapore’s racial harmony could be threatened by malicious foreign influence; two, more than seven in 10 respondents agreed that there should be laws to protect race-based entities from malicious foreign actors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 15 empowers a competent authority to designate a race-based entity if considered necessary or expedient to pre-empt, prevent or reduce any foreign influence that may undermine racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: An entity may be designated by the competent authority if it: one, represents or promotes the social, economic, political, educational, linguistic, cultural or other interests of any race; or two, discusses any issue relating to any race.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We recognise that there is a wide range of entities that engage with race-related issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a policy stance, we will start off in a practical and measured manner by only designating race-based entities assessed to have a higher potential of being vectors for malicious foreign influence, rather than subjecting all race-based entities to the measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will need time to assess the entities in these categories before we can inform them whether they will be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clans and business associations, including those focused on trade promotion that are assessed not to be linked to the Chinese, Malay and Indian races, will not be designated at this juncture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, we do not preclude designating such entities in the future, as the foreign influence landscape evolves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I understand that there may be some anxiety amongst business associations as to whether they will be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will make two points: first, designation is not a reflection of any wrongdoing by the entity and should not be perceived as such; second, business associations and organisations whose objects, purposes or activities do not relate to any race, will not be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Each designation decision will be made holistically and on its own merits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The list of designated entities will be made public to promote transparency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These baseline measures are similar to those that all religious groups under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act have to comply with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The disclosure requirements will be set out in the subsidiary legislation and will take reference from the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, designated entities will need to disclose foreign affiliations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This refers to arrangements or agreements where foreign persons or organisations have a position of control or power over the race-based entity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Third, designated entities will need to disclose the leadership composition of their governing body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Responsible officers include the chairperson of the board of directors, the chief executive officer or the company secretary of a company; or the president, secretary and treasurer of a society; and two, the majority of the governing body, or anyone exercising functions analogous to a governing body member, are required to be Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For the first three measures, I wish to highlight that the focus is on disclosure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There will not be a blanket prohibition for designated entities to stop accepting foreign donations or to end foreign affiliations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They just need to disclose these matters on an annual basis to MHA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government is prepared to grant exemptions to specific baseline measures on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 32 provides an avenue for designated entities to apply to the Minister for exemption from some or all of the baseline measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is a similar process for religious groups under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: All entities will be notified ahead of being designated and will be provided time to submit their representations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The intent is to pre-empt, prevent or reduce any malicious foreign influence affecting the entity which may undermine racial harmony and present a threat to public peace and public order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is the same threshold for a foreign influence Restraining Order to be issued under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These stepped-up measures against a designated entity may do one or more of the following: (a) Prohibit the entity from accepting any donation from a specified foreign principal or any anonymous donation; (b) Require the entity to return or dispose of any donation from a specified foreign principal or any anonymous donation; (c) Prohibit the entity from forming or maintaining a specified foreign affiliation; and/or (d) Prohibit the entity from appointing, admitting or retaining a specified individual – whether or not the individual is a Singapore Citizen – as a member of its governing body, or require the entity to remove any individual who is not or who ceases to be a Singapore Citizen as a member of its governing body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These powers will, amongst others, mitigate the risk of Singapore Citizens becoming proxies for a foreign principal to exert influence over the race-based entity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Of note, while this policy intent is also relevant for religious groups, such a lever is not currently present in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act will be amended to introduce a similar provision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Foreign influence Restraining Orders will also be reviewed by the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony, and must be confirmed by the President, similar to the racial content Restraining Orders I spoke about earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today, we are introducing the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This Bill was announced by then-Prime Minister Lee in his 2021 National Day Rally Speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At that time, we were in the thick of the COVID-19 pandemic and you might recall that several racist incidents were widely publicised on social media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It reminds us that although Singapore has come a long way in our race relations since our early years, racial harmony is not the natural order of things.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have to continue to work at it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This Bill is the latest in our suite of measures to strengthen social cohesion and safeguard racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is a new Bill but, in fact, much of what is in the Bill is not new.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Similar provisions already exist in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, which was enacted in 1990 and amended in 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will further elaborate on the proposals dealing with the Restraining Order regime and safeguards against foreign influence for race-based entities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Bill will enable the Minister for Home Affairs to make Restraining Orders against persons involved in the communication, production and distribution of content that prejudices the maintenance of racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will complement existing levers, such as the Broadcasting Act and Online Criminal Harms Act, which provide ex-post powers against egregious race-related content on platforms such as social media services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I wish to assure Members that the Government will be very careful when exercising its power to issue Restraining Orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The fact that no Restraining Orders have been issued to date since the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was introduced in 1990 is reflective of this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Restraining Orders are also subject to a variety of safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For instance, they must be reviewed by the Presidential Council for Religious Harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The introduction of the Restraining Order regime is in line with the public's views that racially offensive content should be removed quickly to prevent the erosion of racial harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Restraining Order is intended to provide more levers to preserve our social cohesion, not to silence legitimate opinions on race even if the Government may disagree with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The last proposal in this Bill will introduce safeguards against malicious foreign influence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As we know, Singapore is vulnerable to external actors exerting malicious foreign influence to achieve their own agenda.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They may do so in many ways, for instance, by seeding ideas that are incompatible with our multiracial society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Entities that promote the interests of a racial group or discuss issues relating to race are therefore potential entry points for such malicious foreign influence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We recognise that there is a wide range of entities that engage with race-related issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a policy stance, we will start off in a practical and measured manner by only designating race-based entities assessed to have a higher potential of being vectors for malicious foreign influence, rather than subjecting all race-based entities to the measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will need time to assess these entities in these categories before we can inform them whether they will be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clans and business associations, including those focused on trade promotion, that are assessed to be not linked to the Chinese, Malay and Indian races will not be designated at this juncture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, we do not preclude designating such entities in the future as the foreign influence landscape evolves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I understand that there may be some anxiety amongst business associations as to whether they will be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Here, I would like to make two points.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, business associations and organisations whose objects, purposes or activities do not relate to any race will not be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, designation is not a reflection of any wrongdoing by the entity and should not be perceived as such.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Each designation decision will be made holistically and based on its own merits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The list of the designated entities will be made public to promote transparency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The baseline measures for designated race-based entities are similar to those that all religious groups are currently required to comply with under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Designated entities will need to disclose foreign donations and anonymous donations, foreign affiliations and their leadership compositions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They will also need to comply with certain leadership requirements, such as the requirement for their top office-bearers to be Singapore Citizens or PRs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government is also prepared to grant exemptions to specific baseline measures on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To be clear, the baseline measures for designated race-based entities are meant to be a preventive measure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Being designated does not mean the entity is being targeted or has been compromised by a foreign actor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are also not instructing designated race-based entities to stop receiving foreign donations or to end any foreign affiliations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They just need to disclose these matters on an annual basis to MHA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When subsequently operationalising the Bill, MHA will provide an information kit to designated entities to guide them in complying with the requirements. : Mr Speaker, Sir, racial harmony will always remain a work-in-progress in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We build on efforts and learn from the lessons of the past.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is also our responsibility to plant new seeds in accordance with new circumstances and realities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government will continue to do our part, but it will take a whole-of-society effort to sustain the progress we have made so that future generations of Singaporeans too will enjoy the peace and harmony that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Racial harmony is not something we can take for granted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about creating a society where we all feel at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill possesses the potential to achieve its objectives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, its success depends on how it is implemented and perceived by the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have clarifications about the racial content Restraining Orders in Part 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But like all tools, they need to be handled carefully.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The power of racial content Restraining Orders is undeniable, but with that power comes an inherent challenge: balancing enforcement with the preservation of freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that these orders are not misused to stifle legitimate discourse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These includes artistic expressions, like parodies, satire or critiques of societal issues that touch on race.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While some content may indeed cross the line, how do we draw boundaries between harmful speech and those forms of expression that are vital for a vibrant and open society?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the current approach inadvertently silence voices that challenge the status quo in a way that promotes reflection and growth?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we ensure that these laws do not become a tool for shutting down uncomfortable but necessary conversations about race and identity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to pair these measures with public campaigns that teach empathy, respect and dialogue?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Racial harmony is not just about avoiding offence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about understanding each other's struggles and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond penalties, how does this Bill encourage connection?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Harmony thrives when people see each other as neighbours, not strangers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can this legislation inspire bridge-building between communities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, Singapore's openness is undoubtedly a strength, but it also makes us vulnerable to external risks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Part 4 of the Bill rightly addresses the challenge of foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is critical that we proceed carefully to avoid unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The penalties involved are substantial and this could inadvertently discourage Singaporeans and PRs from stepping forward to take on leadership roles in local associations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that this legislation does not unintentionally deter participation in community and cultural leadership?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, how do we define and differentiate "foreign influence" from "global collaboration"?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many local associations maintain deep historical ties with overseas organisations, preserving our cultural heritage over decades, if not centuries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the broad definition of "foreign affiliation" unintentionally create barriers for such groups?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would this legislation impact non-profit or cultural organisations with harmless international connections?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transparent and proportionate enforcement will be critical to allaying such concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there overlapping provisions and, if so, how will both pieces of legislation complement one another?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clarity is essential to avoid unnecessary duplication of compliance requirements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regular reviews and transparent monitoring will be necessary to ensure the measures effectively strengthen racial harmony without hindering meaningful international partnerships or discouraging our community's engagement with global networks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Offering an alternative to prosecution is a progressive step, but it also raises a few questions too.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we decide who qualifies for this programme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how will it address the underlying prejudices or misunderstandings that led to the offense?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will participants truly understand the importance of racial harmony or will they simply view it as another box to tick?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will grassroots leaders and organisations play a role in shaping or running these programmes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their involvement could bring authenticity and trust to the process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What happens if someone does not complete the programme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be room for appeals or second chances?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how does this initiative fit into the overall Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could it serve as a softer, community-based complement to the more stringent Restraining Orders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, policies alone do not build harmony.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why constructive engagement with the public is so important.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Part 5 of the Bill outlines oversight mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be regular public consultations to ensure these measures remain relevant and effective?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Listening to people's lived experiences can make our policies stronger.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony work with communities on the ground?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Solutions must feel inclusive and co-created, not imposed from above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we make public awareness campaigns engaging for everyone to understand their role in maintaining harmony?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But they also gave rise to a commitment, a collective will, to build something stronger, something lasting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are here today because of the hard work, the courage and the vision of those who came before us, who understood that racial harmony is not just a hope, it is a necessity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, we cannot let these positive numbers lull us into complacency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must strive for an environment where every Singaporean, whether born here or new to our shores, understands that racial harmony is not just a policy – it is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is no place in Singapore for the biases that divide us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must make it clear, now and always, that racism has no place here.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a living, breathing reality that requires constant care, constant work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is an important step, but it is only the beginning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, how do we ensure that the CRI is more than just a programme, but a true opportunity for understanding and healing?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And lastly, how do we engage every member of our community in the ongoing work of nurturing racial harmony?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us remember that true harmony is not just about avoiding conflict.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about building connections, about recognising our shared humanity, acknowledging our differences and yet, seeing what unites us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is often hailed as a model of multiracial harmony.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We owe it to ourselves, to our children and to our future generations to keep moving forward – towards a Singapore where every individual feels seen, heard and valued.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill gives us the tools to make that vision a reality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it is up to us to inspire the kind of harmony that goes beyond legislation, to inspire the kind of harmony that lives in the hearts and minds of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us legislate for harmony, but let us also live it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it is important this Bill fosters racial harmony without unintentionally stifling essential public discourse and silencing marginalised voices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Racial harmony is a cornerstone of our society and I think we all agree that it cannot be achieved through legislation alone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Enduring racial harmony requires genuine understanding and open dialogue among all communities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the broad Ministerial powers under this Bill risk deterring legitimate public discourse that is essential for fostering intercommunal dialogue and strengthen social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For instance, public critiques of systemic discrimination or policies affecting certain racial groups could be misconstrued as vilifying or denigrating others, even when the intent is to raise awareness or advocate for positive change.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Forums discussing global events, like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, or domestic policies such as the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) could risk being labelled as racially inflammatory, despite their role in constructive discourse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is important to distinguish between speech that on one hand, incites hatred and violence, which should be prevented, and speech that fosters understanding and calls out racial inequalities, which we should encourage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Constructive conversations, including in public forums, are necessary for addressing racial issues and strengthening intercommunal trust.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Bill includes defences for private communication and calling out racism in good faith, individuals may still be uncertain about their practical application.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The need to prove good faith intent or the private nature of a conversation could create hesitation to engage in discussions on race.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This uncertainty may discourage open dialogue and cause such conversations to go underground or in echo chambers within the Internet.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that unlike the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, which explicitly prohibits the mixing of religion and politics, this Bill does not contain a similar prohibition on the mixing of race and politics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Foreign influence operations can exploit racial and communal fault lines, destabilising our society and undermining social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Countering foreign interference is a necessary component of maintaining racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ability to monitor and regulate race-based entities, and to take action against harmful external influences, is an important step in protecting Singapore's racial harmony and national security, and I acknowledge the Government's efforts in addressing this issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill introduces measures such as designating entities and issuing Restraining Orders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party supports the inclusion of these provisions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is important, however, that these powers are exercised judiciously, with transparency and accountability to maintain public trust.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ensuring that decisions are seen as fair and impartial will be crucial to the effectiveness and legitimacy of these measures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I support the introduction of the Community Remedial programme, which offers an alternative to prosecution by encouraging participants to reflect on their actions and fostering rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be effective, the programme should engage participants in meaningful dialogue with members of other racial groups, allowing for deeper understanding and reflection on the impact of their actions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will its effectiveness be measured to ensure it leads to genuine rehabilitation and behavioural change?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, the Government feedback unit, Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry (REACH), conducted a public consultation last year, but the feedback collected remains largely opaque, with only summarised data shared publicly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A Select Committee provides a more transparent and rigorous process, allowing for in-depth scrutiny, public engagement and expert input, particularly from minority communities most affected by such legislation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government's Forward Singapore report underscores the need to strengthen our social compact through deeper citizen engagement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, for an issue as fundamental as race relations, bypassing the Select Committee process weakens participatory democracy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A strong democratic system requires more than just electoral participation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It must also ensure meaningful avenues for policy-making input, robust public consultations and rigorous legislative scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should uphold these principles by ensuring that future legislation of similar significance is subject to the full scrutiny of a Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill does this holistically through not just quick and pre-emptive responses, but through community-based approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend MHA for its broad consultation with the public and community leaders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all have a stake in a multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The consultative process for the Bill reflects this priority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the function of the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will replace the Presidential Council for Religious Harmony.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony is supposed to comprise representatives from all major racial and religious communities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Context, considerations and nuances for racial and religious matters will differ.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Representatives from major racial communities may not be best placed to opine on religious matters and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, under section 9 of Schedule 1 on the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony, vacancy among its members does not affect the validity of the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony's proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Presumably, the requirement that representatives from all major racial and religious communities in Singapore are present on the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony are to ensure that perspectives of all communities are considered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the quorum requirement ensures that at least half of members must be present, the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony is also set up such that every member plays an important role in representing their racial or religious community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, under the current Presidential Council for Religious Harmony, there is one representative for each major religious group.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is difficult to imagine a decision concerning a particular religious group without the representative from that group present.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without being prescriptive as to the procedures of the Presidential Council, can the Minister share if the chairperson of the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony should ensure the presence of representatives when decisions affecting their communities are deliberated and made?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share why the President does not have the discretion to vary the direction when it comes to the extension of a Restraining Order?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what measures are available to address the root causes of racist conduct which necessitate the Restraining Order in the first place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When it comes to offences relating to race, the Bill introduces the possibility of community remediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Individuals subject to a Restraining Order may similarly require intervention to address ideologies and misconceptions underlying the conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will be taken to address the root causes of the conduct attracting the Restraining Order?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on remediation for serious offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under CRI-Race, persons who have engaged in conduct prejudicial to racial harmony can take remedial action for their conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Completing the programme can be taken into account by the Public Prosecutor in deciding whether to prosecute a race-related offence under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Underlying the CRI-Race is the principle of restorative justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The offender will have the opportunity to learn and make amends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This restores any damaged community relations and can even serve to strengthen ties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the CRI-Race will not be offered if the offence is egregious.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has stated that criminal prosecution will be pursued to send a signal of non-tolerance for serious racial offending.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that prosecution may be necessary in serious cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Appropriate punishment is also a form of repairing community relations by reinforcing healthy norms on race relations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, punishment and rehabilitation are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even serious offenders who are jailed, must eventually return and re-integrate into society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For these serious offenders, time in prison alone does not necessarily mean they will emerge with any better understanding of race relations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It may be even more important for these serious offenders to participate in programmes targeted to address deep-seated ideologies and misconceptions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How do we ensure that their time in prison does not have the adverse effect of radicalising these individuals even further?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With globalisation and the spread of different cultures and information, both within countries and across borders, even more sensitivity is needed to deal with these topics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If and when discussions on race and religion cross certain boundaries and cause hurt, disharmony, hostility or even violence among communities, it would be appropriate for the state to intervene in the interest of maintaining public order and peace.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill that we are debating today needs to strike a fair and reasonable balance between the freedom of speech and expression and the preservation of public order, peace and racial harmony.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) supports laws to protect our order and peace in our multiracial and multi-religious country.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Harmonious and peaceful relations between different races and religions is something that we should never take for granted in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we also value the fact that freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right enshrined in our Constitution.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is freedom of speech that allows for creativity, the exchange of ideas and opinions and improvements beneficial to society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also freedom of speech that allows us to seek accountability from those in power.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While discussions involving race can be sensitive, but honest and responsible discussions on racial relations and topics are necessary for better inter-racial understanding and mutual respect.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
