text: We must not allow such discussions to be stifled and driven underground by overly restrictive legislation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are, therefore, naturally concerned that the Government will use such executive powers to further restrict what Singaporeans can do or say.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would like to seek the Minister's clarification on if and, if so, how, the use of this Act will be calibrated to ensure that a fair and appropriate balance will be struck between the right of Singaporeans to their freedom of speech and expression, and our public order and peace.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will set out a few examples here to frame this debate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is the incident involving Mr Shaik Amar who made comments about EIP on social media in July 2024.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He had commented that EIP does not benefit ethnic minority households and only causes them significant financial detriment when they sell their flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Assuming the answer is yes, does this mean that there are potentially cases that could and, in practice, would attract both a Correction Direction under POFMA and a Restraining Order under this Bill if the conditions are satisfied?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second is in relation to conflicts, such as the Israel-Hamas war.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such comments may be made online by a very large number of people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Considering that, what factors will push a case beyond the tipping point, such that a Restraining Order will be imposed?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, considering that millions of comments are posted every day on social media, practically speaking, how does the Ministry intend to monitor these comments?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much manpower and spending by the Ministry is justifiable to monitor comments like these?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would individuals committing such acts be subject to a Restraining Order or prosecuted under clause 40 of the Bill?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in 2017, Muslim imam Mr Nalla Mohamed Abdul Jameel Abdul Malik, was convicted under section 298A for promoting enmity between different religious groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2015, Mr Amos Yee was convicted under section 298 of wounding the religious feelings of Christians for describing Jesus Christ in an offensive manner.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other cases, the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) chose not to prosecute.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These include Ms Amy Cheong's hurtful remarks online regarding Malay weddings in 2013 and Ms Sangeetha Thanapal's claim in 2018 that casual racism was common.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the enactment of this Bill lead to more types of actions and speech attracting Restraining Orders or prosecutions under clause 40?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister issue Restraining Orders to Ms Amy Cheong or Ms Sangeetha Thanapal under the Bill if they said the same things today?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notably, Ms Sangeetha Thanapal's comments had been made overseas, which is now explicitly covered by the Bill under clause 38.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, we note that under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, the Council has 30 days to make its recommendations to the President; under this Bill, that period has been extended to 44 days.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that a Restraining Order will take immediate effect upon its service on the person restrained before the Council makes its recommendations, we would like to ask for the reason for this extension from 30 to 44 days.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are also concerned about the effect of clause 8(2)(d) and (e) on journalists and editors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 8(2)(d) can prohibit a person from editing or contributing to "any publication".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 8(2)(e) goes further to prohibit a person from holding office in any editorial board.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether our concerns are valid and how these two clauses will be used?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   For a long time, race and religion have been sensitive topics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When discussions about race and religion lead to disharmony, hostility or even violence between communities, it is appropriate for the Government to intervene to maintain public order and peace.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill, being read the second time today, needs to strike a good balance between freedom of speech and maintaining public order, peace and racial harmony.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore is multiracial and multi-religious society, and our racial and religious harmony has not come easily and cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP, therefore, supports using legislation to maintain harmony between races and religions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we also cherish the freedom of speech granted to us by the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Freedom of speech is a fundamental right that promotes creativity, social progress and the exchange of ideas.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also allows us to hold those in power accountable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While discussions involving race can be sensitive, it is necessary to discuss racial issues in an honest and responsible manner to promote understanding and mutual respect between races.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These sensitive racial topics include the impact on housing prices by HDB's EIP, our country's CMIO racial classification system, the racial distribution of death row inmates and the deployment of Malay National Servicemen.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While not everyone will agree with these statements, discussing these topics in a rational, responsible, non-malicious and non-hostile manner can promote national and social development.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Minister can clarify how this Bill will strike a fair and appropriate balance between citizens' right to freedom of speech and public order and peace. : Deputy Speaker, PSP has serious concerns that the powers under this Bill will dampen important discussions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have provided several examples of speech and actions, which I hope that the Minister can clarify whether the powers in this Bill will be used against such speech or actions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Protests are only allowed at Hong Lim Park and protest permits are not granted for sensitive topics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ability of Singaporeans to freely express themselves is already very circumscribed and limited by existing laws.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we hope greater clarity can be given in order not to dampen reasonable discussions or expressions involving race.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, racial harmony, just like our peace and stability, is not something that we can take for granted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This trend underscores the need for proactive measures to address the underlying causes of racial tensions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill, thus, presents an opportunity to strengthen our commitment in fostering a cohesive and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Before I seek specific clarifications in this Bill, I would like to highlight the importance of: firstly, the roles that we all play to maintain racial harmony; and secondly, the continued importance of our existing race-based integration policies and organisations which complements the objectives set out in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While I applaud that the Bill introduces legal tools, such as ROs and community remedial measures, I believe that we must also tackle the root causes of racial tensions and, at the heart of it, racism.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We as a society must do our part to safeguard against prejudices and discrimination through indirect means, like casual racism.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, it remains a pervasive issue, often dismissed as unintentional or harmless.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, research shows that such behaviors perpetuate discrimination and exclusion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whether in a family setting or workplace, this must be addressed with both clarity and conviction.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The work needed to maintain racial harmony cannot be left to the enforcement mechanism in this Bill or any other piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must begin in our schools, our workplaces and our homes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, we can introduce stronger education initiatives, like compulsory racial sensitivity training in schools and workplaces, to counter unconscious biases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At workplaces, we can encourage positive interracial interactions by fostering a culture of understanding and empathy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Businesses can also establish concrete anti-discrimination policies that evolve with and reflect current societal attitudes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When every individual, regardless of race, language or religion, feels respected and valued, then racial harmony is not just enforced, but deeply ingrained in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, while we aspire to be colour blind, we cannot close our eyes to the realities on the ground nor abandon the foundations that have been built by generations before us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our policies remain crucial to maintaining racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, our self-help groups, continue to mobilise resources and deliver targeted interventions along communal lines.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having volunteered in this space for many years before I became a Member of Parliament, I have seen how self-help groups provide an additional avenue for assistance and navigate through cultural or religious sensitivities that had risen.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, policies like EIP go beyond housing but right to the heart of our integration as a society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not just about putting different people from different races together in the same block or in the same precinct.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It shapes generations and how we mould ourselves together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once people of different races live together, they become neighbours and they become friends, their children grow up together, they help one another and learn to live together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regardless of whether we speak less of our mother tongues or erase race from our identity cards, our race and identity stays with us wherever we go.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can have various legislations or campaigns but, ultimately, racial harmony depends on each and every one of us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is why, while this Bill grants significant powers to intervene in racial disputes, a community-led approach will be more effective in supplementing and fostering long-term racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: No amount of laws can change the heart of a community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With that I move to my clarifications, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My first set of clarifications relate to the provisions that protect our racial organisations against foreign influence trying to exploit racial lines or undermine our racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill draws parallels with FICA in respect of Restraining Orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under FICA, such interference includes actions that incite or are likely to incite feelings of enmity, hatred or ill will between different groups in Singapore, endangering public peace and order.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just like hon Member Mr Yip Hon Weng, I join him in his clarifications on the overlap between FICA and this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why are similar provisions required in two separate legislations and whether given the possible overlap, how will the Ministry appropriately ensure that the powers in both legislations will be exercised judiciously?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, its provisions remain a critical safeguard against foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What about individual businesses that do not belong to such associations but have deep links to foreign organisations?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, can the Minister assure the House that MHA will continually review the list by monitoring race-based organisations and their activities?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, will there be an avenue for reporting by members of the public or whistle-blowers for MHA to follow up on investigation or further assessment?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similar restorative justice programmes exist globally, such as in New Zealand's family group and conferences and Canada’s indigenous sentencing circles.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Locally, we have seen success with community-based sentencing in other areas, such as youth rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By emphasising rehabilitation over punishment, CRI aligns with our broader goal of fostering understanding and harmony.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the intended outcomes for CRI for the perpetrators or the individuals or the community affected by the offence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate that the Minister has stated that CRI will involve creating awareness on the impact on affected community, making amends or amendments or suitable reparations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And thirdly, for such CRI, would the close or immediate family members of the offender be involved or be a participant as well?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because this may help the rehabilitation of the offender on a long-term basis if his close family or home environment is also taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fourthly, to build public trust in CRI, we must ensure transparency and rigor in its implementation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the measures that the Ministry will take in this regard?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would there be clear published guidelines on the detailed criteria for eligibility and programme requirements for CRI?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whether there will be public awareness campaigns to educate the public on the benefits of restorative justice and reconciliation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Minister ensure that proper resources are allocated and provided to the necessary organisations that will be implementing the CRI?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a Malay-Muslim and a minority in Singapore, we benefit from the safeguarding of racial harmony, which is a cornerstone of our country, so that there will be no repeat of the racial riots that our people experienced during our country's early years of independence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here, I would like to share the story of my late mother during those racial riots, an experience that taught me a valuable lesson.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My late mother witnessed the procession to commemorate Prophet Muhammad's birthday in the early 1960s when racial riots broke out in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At that time, my grandfather, who was a police officer, was part of the police contingent participating in the procession.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My mother and her three older sisters, along with my grandparents, boarded a bus to return home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This bus was also carrying several other passengers of various races – there were Chinese, Malays and even a Sikh.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the way home, their bus came to a halt when the rioters blocked their bus and began throwing bottles and stones at it.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At that moment, everyone on the bus was worried about their safety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there was only one thing in their minds regardless of whether they were Malay, Chinese or Indian.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They all just want to get home safely.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Eventually, a few young men got off the bus to clear a path for their vehicle to drive quickly away from that place.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This incident left a profound impact on my mother, who was still very young at the time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My mother advised me: although we were of different races and religions, all of us in Singapore are like passengers in the same bus, heading in one direction towards the same destination.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we must take care of each other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since young, she instilled in me the importance of racial harmony in Singapore's multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I welcome any legislation that will continue to maintain and safeguard racial harmony in our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, Singapore can take a more proactive approach towards racial harmony that goes beyond law enforcement and fosters a society built on mutual understanding, dialogue and integration. : Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, in my Malay speech, I shared the account of my late mother whose family was stuck in a bus right in the middle of the 1960s racial riots.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The passengers in the bus consisted of families from various races – Malay, Chinese and Indian.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At that time, when crowds ran amok and chaos engulfed them, the only thing that the passengers wanted was safety and safe passage home for everyone on the bus.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They did not care if the rioters outside were of any particular race.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just like the passengers on that bus, we fellow Singaporeans must continue to take care of one another, regardless of how we look, the language we speak or from where our families first originated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The world is increasingly conducive for the divisive.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are all on the same boat, heading in one direction towards the same destination.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The multiracial and multi-cultural character of my country has made us somewhat skeptical of those who preach the superiority and exclusiveness of one culture and one race.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a multiracial society, one soon learns that no one people has a monopoly of wisdom and that one's own culture is not without flaws.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But I have some questions and concerns to the proposed provisions in this Bill relating to clans and business organisations which would be designated as race-based entities under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: CNA reported that according to MHA, organisations that promote the interest of a racial group or subgroup are potential entry points for such influence, and that entities may be designated if their objectives and activities represent the interest of any race or issues relating to it and that "designation is deemed necessary or expedient to preempt, prevent or reduce any foreign influence that may undermine racial harmony in Singapore." Mr Deputy Speaker, while I agree that clans and business associations linked to races should be protected from foreign political influence and interference, I am concerned with the potential impact the new rules may have on our clan associations and other race-based associations whose focus may be cultural and economic and not political.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clauses 18 to 22 of this Bill provide for regulations imposing reporting obligations on designated entities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 18(1) requires that designated entities will generally be required to report the foreign donations and anonymous donations that they accept, subject to the regulations to be provided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 18(2) sets out various matters that may be prescribed by the regulations to be included in the reports to be submitted by designated entities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They include the classes of foreign donations and anonymous donations that need not be reported.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would these be categorised by a monetary limit?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 19(1) requires designated entities to report their foreign affiliations according to the subsidiary legislations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clause 19(2) sets out various matters to be prescribed by the regulations which must be included in such reports by the designated entities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It would also enable Members of Parliament to appreciate MHA's concern about the risk of foreign interference on such clans and associations, leading to MHA tabling such requirements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that MHA will also be empathetic to organisational constraints, especially in smaller clans and business associations, when regulations are introduced for easier administrative compliance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, many of these office-bearers and members are volunteers and staff support may be limited, especially for the smaller clans and associations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I say this because there are possibly mutual benefits from such donations if such clans and associations find it difficult to raise funds while foreign businesses may find that it is a good marketing avenue for their businesses and products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While MHA can follow up on declared foreign entities, if it deems necessary, I hope that there will not be unnecessary stigma relating to foreign donations per se as long as there is no political interference.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to know whether the financial contributions to joint projects between local clans or business organisations and their foreign counterparts come under the clauses of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, I am concerned that their inclusion may discourage joint projects which may be beneficial to the development of our local clans or business organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clauses 23 to 26 of this Bill impose basic leadership restrictions on such designated entities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The provisions require that more than half of the total number of seats on the governing body of any designated entity must be occupied or held by Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For governing bodies with fewer than three seats, all of them must be occupied or held by Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Responsible officers of designated entities must be Singapore Citizens or Singapore PRs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While their support and participation in clans and business organisations should be encouraged and allowed, the leadership of such entities should remain with those with no other nationality than that of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill, but I have some questions and concerns about the provisions in the Bill regarding clan associations and business associations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I declare that I am an honorary advisor to the Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: According to the Bill, clan associations and business associations will be required to declare details of foreign donations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many clan associations are already facing numerous challenges in their operations, including attracting new generations of members, maintaining the associations' operations and ensuring their continued relevance and contribution to a modern Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, the process of declaring foreign donations should not create additional administrative burdens for them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that MHA will show more empathy towards smaller clan associations and business associations when implementing these new regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, many association directors and members are volunteers, and these associations have limited manpower and resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Severe penalties on unintentional oversights will put significant pressure on these organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, donations from foreign clan associations, business associations or foreign counterparts may provide support for local associations or business organisations that are short of funds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, donations also give foreign companies more exposure in the market.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is a principle that has anchored our social stability and will continue to be vital as our society becomes more interconnected.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of clear measures to address emerging risks is timely and necessary.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we implement this Bill, it is important to provide clarity for trade associations and foreign chambers of commerce so that they can continue their work in strengthening economic partnerships and fostering international collaboration.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that these business-focused organisations continue to be able to operate effectively within this framework and reinforce Singapore's standing as a trusted global business hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I therefore have five clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, one key area requiring clarification is the classification of trade associations under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, within Singapore Business Federation, we have representation from Singapore Chinese Chamber, Indian and Malay Chamber of Commerce, American Chamber of Commerce, China Enterprises Association, European Chamber of Commerce and the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Each of them plays crucial roles in facilitating trade, investment and cross-border business relations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These associations serve an economic purpose, focusing on bilateral trade policies, market access and regulatory advocacy, and not promoting any racial agenda.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification is related to restrictions on foreign donations and affiliations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under this Bill, such funding could be classified as foreign donations and subject to regulatory scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if a multinational corporation sponsors a networking event hosted by a trade association, would this be deemed a foreign donation requiring disclosure or approval?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If so, even though the Bill does not prohibit a designated trade association from accepting such sponsorships, the compliance implications for multinational enterprises could be significant.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Their internal risk assessment may classify sponsorship of a designated entity as a potential regulatory exposure, leading them to reconsider or, in the worst case, withdraw financial support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This could in turn discourage multinational companies (MNCs) from engaging with trade associations in Singapore, limiting the ability of these associations to organise industry events, foster business collaborations and advocate for trade and investment growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another common practice is industry collaborations between local and foreign business councils.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if a Singapore-based association receives funding from an ASEAN business counterpart, would that funding be classified as a foreign donation?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The implications of such a designation could hinder industry collaboration across markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While the intent is to prevent undue foreign influence, this could pose practical challenges for foreign chambers and trade associations that rely on senior representatives from multinational corporations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These individuals bring industry expertise, strengthen bilateral ties and advocate for business-friendly policies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Would such advocacy be hindered by restrictions on non-Singaporean leadership in trade organisations?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister therefore consider flexibility in leadership requirements for trade associations that do not engage in racial or political advocacy?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, I would like to seek clarification on the subject of foreign affiliations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In today’s fast-changing world, trade associations must remain nimble, flexible and responsive to support businesses and strengthen international partnerships.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Trade associations frequently sign MOUs and establish partnerships with overseas trade bodies, embassies and government-linked investment agencies to promote cultural, as well as business exchanges, facilitate trade and strengthen international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These agreements are a regular and necessary part of global business engagement, allowing Singapore companies to expand their networks and access new markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under this Bill, would such partnerships be subject to foreign influence reporting requirements and if so, what criteria would determine whether a Memorandum of Understanding or collaboration falls under these regulations?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Clear and well-defined guidelines will enable them to continue fostering global collaboration seamlessly while upholding Singapore's strong social fabric.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As these organisations focus on business, trade facilitation and international collaboration, it is important they understand the basis for their classification under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If an association appeals against its designation, clear guidelines are essential to ensure transparency in classification criteria and assessment factors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will help trade associations operate with confidence while ensuring compliance.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I ask the Minister whether these classifications will be made transparent in advance and what the appeal process for exemptions will entail.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Barring my clarifications, I fully support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, on the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill has several aims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, the views expressed in my speech today are my own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a risk that foreign entities may attempt or may already have attempted to channel their race-based agenda through Singapore-based entities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry has informed this House that in the run-up to this Bill, it has consulted race-based organisations that it intends to designate for the new transparency requirements and that they understood the need for these new obligations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As mentioned by others before me, not all foreign connections are malign.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the ground, it is quite common to see race-based organisations having reciprocal relationships with like-minded organisations in other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Chinese-based organisations, these like-minded organisations may reside in Malaysia, Brunei and China.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such relationships enrich the breadth of engagement on shared interests and increase access to resources for charitable activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such connections also enhance people-to-people ties across national borders, which is to be encouraged from a foreign affairs perspective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the implementation of this Bill, such benign foreign relationships should be allowed to continue and flourish.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   On this matter, I would like to share some observations about foreign connections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the ground, it is quite common to see race-based organisations having reciprocal relationships with race-based organisations in other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Chinese-based organisations, they may reside in Malaysia, Brunei and China.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such relationships enrich the breadth of engagement on shared interests and increase access to resources for charitable activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From a foreign affairs perspective, such connections also enhance people-to-people ties across national borders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should allow such benign foreign relationships to continue and flourish. : I now move to the roles to be played by the President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These provisions are covered in both the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill and the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such discretion will be available if the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony disagrees with the Minister's decision to issue a Restraining Order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This discretionary power sought to be given to the EP goes to the fundamentals of governance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am sure the Government will agree with me that the responsibility of maintaining racial harmony and law and order lies with the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While all of us have a part to play, the Government is responsible for this outcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is publicly accountable for this key performance indicator to Singaporeans through Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not the EP's responsibility to maintain public peace and public order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He is not answerable to Parliament in any way.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the proposed mechanism for the President to review the Minister's Orders carries several significant risks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Imagine a scenario where the Minister issues a Restraining Order which the Presidential Council disagrees with, following which the EP then decides to also disagree with the Minister and cancels the Restraining Order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I pause here to point out that although some of us may think that such a scenario of both the Presidential Council and the President breaking ranks with the Cabinet is unlikely, this is exactly what the Bills today permit to happen.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Returning to the scenario of the President cancelling the Restraining Order, let us say it subsequently turns out that the organisation concerned had truly become a proxy for a hostile foreign actor, or race relations deteriorate sharply, proving that the Minister was justified in issuing the Restraining Order in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When Singaporeans question the decision-making process, the Government can justifiably say that it correctly issued the Restraining Order but since the EP decided to cancel it, the Government is not to be blamed for the bad outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a separate note, I am also concerned about the grave implications of bringing the President into such decisions involving ethnicity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As our founding Prime Minister has said, the President is a symbol of unity and the personification of the state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, that is the President's central and defining role.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To require him to make hard decisions on matters involving ethnicity will detract from his role as a unifying figure above politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill envisages the President possibly confronting the Cabinet on decisions that that affect influential race-based organisations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further complicating the matter is that the presidency already has a defined racial dimension due to the reserve presidency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Imagine a scenario if a President were to cancel a Minister's Restraining Order relating to an organisation of the President's own ethnic roots.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even if the President were to do so for objective reasons, would it be perceived as objective?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a scenario could be divisive and highly damaging, not just for the presidency as an institution, but for race relations in general.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill, my party colleagues, Gerald Giam and Dennis Tan, have raised questions and concerns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lines may also get blurred in situations where racial and religious differences could be mixed up, blended together or misunderstood.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even as we endeavour to promote racial and religious harmony, we must be mindful of how we can better integrate foreigners, from foreign employees to PRs and new citizens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those of us who grow up in Singapore, attend local schools and have the benefit of years of national education, you can say that it is almost in our DNA to understand the absolute importance and duty that we all have to maintain racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How about those who have joined us as adults?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we help them to reach a higher level of understanding about cultural nuances and mutual respect, and be able to integrate and assimilate into Singapore society?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could we re-look at how we can build and improve on the educational and learning journeys for new citizens, and also extend to those who are joining as PRs?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our national pledge continues to remind Singaporeans of the need to remain united "regardless of race, language or religion".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now that we are 60 years into our nation-building journey, language is thankfully no longer something that divides Singaporeans, with high English literacy rates and perhaps Singlish being something that unite Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we look to the future, it is my wish that we may one day be able to look beyond race or religion as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, we will still need to be aware and be alert for the other ways which malicious actors, whether foreign or local, can try to carve out fault-lines within our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could include the exploitation of differences in socio-economic levels across our society, as well as attempts to fan xenophobic sentiments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   As we look into the future, it is my wish that we may one day be able to look beyond race or religion as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, we will still need to be aware and be on the alert for the other ways which malicious actors, whether foreign or local, can try to carve out fault-lines within our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could include the exploitation of differences in socio-economic levels across our society as well as attempts to fan xenophobic sentiments. : We should also be cognisant that we ourselves do not overly focus on and draw our own fault lines unnecessarily and cause alarm.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, I had paid attention to the Board Diversity Index that is developed by the Singapore Institute of Directors because of the useful insights that we can draw about the diversity efforts amongst our corporations here.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to be aware that being overly sensitive or in today's parlance, too "woke" without the proper context or understanding, can also cause problems for our society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I think many of us here today are agreed, and I certainly am of the view, that every civilised society has some measure of censorship in it.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It should not be the case that hate speech is allowed to run unchecked in society just because we want to adhere to some imagined or theoretical principle on freedom of speech.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, as it is the case with most things, the most extreme cases of racially harmful content are arguably the easiest ones to address.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Where it is quite clear that offence has been caused and is intended, and maliciously phrased expressions and slurs are used, it is relatively easy for society to come together and band against these acts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The problem, however, lies in the grey areas where, for example, it is not immediately clear whether the acts in question are likely to incite "enmity, hatred, ill will or hostility” against a particular race or “insult, vilify, denigrate, threaten or abuse” another race, as these terms are set out in clauses 8 and 40 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate that the Government does not have an easy task.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Overly strict measures could suppress future dialogue while inaction might encourage irresponsible and harmful behaviour.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is a matter of particular concern to Singapore’s arts community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our arts and cultural groups have long been engaged in thoughtful, critical and necessary conversations about identity, history and race.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If we truly believe in an inclusive and harmonious society, then we must also believe in the power of art, storytelling and critical discourse to bring us closer together.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The question of the extent to which the state should intervene in censorship of the arts is not a new one and it is one that has been addressed by all the previous arts Nominated Members of Parliament at one point or another.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I, too, would like to add my voice to theirs in the context of the Bill that we are debating today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, the Schedule to the Bill only refers to Council members as being “representatives of all major racial and religious communities” and “persons who have distinguished themselves in public service or community relations.” The Council has very wide powers to review racial content Restraining Orders and it is heartening to see that the views of the Minister will be subject to some amount of independent oversight by the Council and the President.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A common refrain amongst the arts community – and I, too, feel this way sometimes when dealing with bureaucracies – is that administrators with little interest in or knowledge of the arts may not have a good understanding of how artistic production takes place, why artists behave in the way that they do, what artists intend to achieve and why the preservation of their voices is important.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Artist representation on the Council is not only desirable, I would go so far as to say it is essential to maintaining public confidence and providing assurance that this new proposed law both safeguards the space for artistic expression while protecting racial harmony.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, in cases where the contentious material is a painting, would the Council seek expert opinions from senior artists, art historians and academics specialising in the visual arts?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the work in question is a literary piece, would the Council then engage with experienced publishers, authors and editors to ensure a well-rounded and informed evaluation?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Schedule to the Bill states that Council members and officers must keep meeting discussions confidential except when sharing with the President, Cabinet, Minister, other Council members or officers, or if they are expressly authorised to make disclosures by the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One strength of this Bill is that it acknowledges the complexity of racially motivated harmful acts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In introducing community remedial programmes in clause 41, it recognises that the remedies for racial intolerance are not to be found only in criminal sanctions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we are better served as a community by ongoing initiatives that seek to rehabilitate and educate.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar spirit, if we regularly make the deliberations of the Council public, this could serve as a very powerful educational tool for the broader community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would not only foster greater transparency but also prompt deeper public engagement and feedback on the decisions that are made.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of input would offer authorities valuable insights into contemporary cultural standards.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It will help them to ensure that their decisions remain attuned to the evolving sentiments of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be seeing regulations which offer examples and guiding principles?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Restraining Orders can be used to prohibit the communication or distribution of “information and material”.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Read in its entirety, these works can be removed from circulation altogether if the Minister is satisfied that the conditions in clause 8(1) are met.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I think that clear examples will be helpful to minimise subjective interpretation and assure the arts community that legitimate artistic works will not fall afoul of the law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister also clarify how the phrase “likely to commit” in clause 8(1) will be construed?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Restraining Orders can be issued if the Minister is “satisfied” that a person is “likely” to commit offences.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is clearly a pre-emptive power and one that should be exercised very carefully.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It should not be the case that art works, books or plays that critically examine racial issues could be banned or censored based on mere speculation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify whether specific guidelines will be used to determine when an artistic work might be regarded as “information or material” connected to acts that are “likely” to cause racial disharmony?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Under this clause, an offence is committed if a person incites enmity, hatred, ill will, hostility, contempt or ridicule against a racial group in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The offence applies if the person knows that their actions are likely to cause this effect.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, a defence under clause 8(6), if the accused person can show that he pointed out the offending matters in good faith and to bring about a removal of those matters.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the strict wording of the Bill, it seems possible that if an artist were to produce, say, a video work about racial tensions in Singapore’s history, or if a theatre company stages a play on colonial era racial policies, that these works might be at risk of being deemed to “incite feelings of ill will.” Let me give the Members a more specific example.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The late artist Lee Wen’s “Journey of a Yellow Man” is a well-known performance art series in Singapore’s art history.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is a work that is studied by art historians and is taught to art students.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is part of the collection of the National Gallery Singapore and it is also a part of other prominent collections overseas.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Lee Wen himself was awarded the Cultural Medallion in 2005.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The work, if Members have not seen it, involves the artist, Lee Wen, a man who is of Chinese ethnicity, covering himself with yellow paint and placing himself into deliberate encounters and situations all over the world.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are then photographed, filmed or sometimes witnessed by an audience.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As explained by the Singapore Art Museum, “the body of work is an exploration of identity and ethnic and cultural stereotypes.” If we apply clause 40(1) to this body of work, it is possible to form the view that Lee, if he were alive today, might be considered as having knowingly ridiculed Chinese ethnicity.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He would have accordingly committed an offence under clause 40(1) when exhibiting his work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could he then rely on the defence in clause 40(6)?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the wording of the Bill, I believe it is not so clear.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Art historians would certainly argue that the work was made in “good faith” but can it be said to have been made or displayed “in order to bring about a removal of the feelings of ridicule?” Well, I would say yes, on balance, but I would also mention that this message is not immediately apparent from the images that are presented in the body of work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Certainly, the works are Lee’s expression of his frustration at being racially stereotyped when he was overseas, but can we say from simply looking at the work that there is a clear enough expression of a desire to bring about the “removal of ridicule”?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Lee’s own declarations may not necessarily shed light on the matter either.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here is an example of something Lee himself has said on the topic in a 1994 artist statement.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Yellow is the colour of the sun, the colour of the moon, the colour of the river that runs in the old country.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is the spirit of nobility, the glow of precious gold.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The warmth and abundance of harvest, the power and faith in temples.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a different sense, yellow can also be the colour of dangerous hazards, confidential secrets, pornography and vices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is also the colour of the persecuted and the oppressed.” So, as you can see, in the realm of art, messaging is often nuanced, layered and open to interpretation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Audiences are invited to engage critically and to interpret the works in their own way.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is what art is all about and why it is so powerful and why we value it.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many artistic works critically examine race, social injustice and history.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These should not be viewed at the get-go as acts of hostility but rather, as efforts to foster deeper understanding.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We do not have a blanket exemption or protection for artistic works, but we must protect our ability to discuss and reflect on history without fear of heightened state intervention.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Racial harmony is indeed the cornerstone of our society, but true harmony is achieved through through open and meaningful dialogue.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Racial harmony has always been a fundamental pillar of our nation’s success.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, we have fostered a culture of mutual respect and understanding among our diverse, multi-ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, in an evolving social landscape marked by the rise of digital media and increasing external influences, it is imperative to adopt new measures that safeguard the delicate balance of our multicultural fabric.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is a timely and necessary step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One, could the Minister of State please elaborate on how the Presidential Council of Racial and Religious Harmony will engage with organisations that have racial affiliations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Council primarily serve an advisory role, or will it have the authority to issue specific guidelines and recommendations that businesses or institutions must adhere to?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please clarify the criteria used to determine when an entity falls within the scope of such orders?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: What safeguards exist to ensure that organisations have the right to appeal or challenge these orders without undue disruption to their operations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister please explain the eligibility criteria for participation and whether completion of the programme will be considered in determining future regulatory actions against offenders.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, how can entities contribute to the broader objectives of such initiatives, potentially as partners in promoting racial harmony?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Four, can the Minister please provide more details on the penalties for non-compliance with the Bill's provisions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government ensure these penalties are proportionate and do not unduly burden businesses?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please clarify what criteria will define an organisation as a "race-based entity"?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government balance the need for transparency with the operational realities of organisations engaged in international collaborations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify the criteria for evaluating foreign donations or affiliations that may be deemed politically or racially sensitive?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Six, the Bill introduces stricter oversight of business associations with racial ties.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please elaborate on how the Government plans to balance regulatory oversight with the operational needs of businesses and chambers of commerce, particularly those engaged in cross-border partnerships?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government address concerns about potential competitive disadvantages for designated race-based entities especially the smaller ones, now that they have additional regulatory requirements and disclosure obligations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on support for businesses, given that the leadership composition rules for designated race-based entities may require significant changes to organisational structures and processes, will the Government consider providing a transition allowance?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, how much time will be given to affected organisations to comply with the new requirements and what support or resources will be made available to help them navigate these changes, without undue disruption to their operations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While this Bill introduces additional compliance requirements for business organisations, it also provides an opportunity for them to contribute meaningfully to our shared national goal of racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that through collaborative efforts, businesses, community groups and the Government can work together to uphold our social cohesion.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In Malay, please. :   Mr Speaker, racial harmony is the cornerstone of Singapore's social stability and prosperity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Although our hearts may differ, shaped by our respective cultural tapestries and ethnic traditions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: As the Malay proverb goes, we all have black hair (birds of a feather).

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is an appropriate measure for our country in order to preserve racial harmony, social stability, a united people as well as national cohesion.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It also creates a fair and just society that views everyone equally regardless of race and one that fosters inclusivity and accords respect and appreciation to all races.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important because Singapore, as an open economy, is also exposed to and not immune to, various external elements and influences.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, with the influence of social media, this Bill needs to be holistic in order to curb news, narratives and perceptions that are false and dangerous, which can trigger misunderstanding, hatred and division between races.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, as a young nation where many of our ancestors were early immigrants and traders, and where our family histories and ethnic traditions may still share intertwined aspects of history, culture and race from China, India and the Malay Archipelago, in these 60 years since Singapore's Independence, there are also many more unique features and local contexts that the people need to consider together.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We must not allow any avenue and opportunity for extreme opinions, which can result in discrimination and racial provocations taking root and permeate our society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This does not mean that we should avoid celebrating our respective racial identities that are rich with diversity and history, or shy away from honest discussions about issues of importance to each race.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: For everything that is allowed to develop in our multiracial and multi-ethnic society, we will need to consider the local context, culture, etiquette, history, harmony and legislation. : Mr Speaker, in English, please.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few clarifications in three broad parts for the Minister, as part of this proposed Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is to reassure us that sufficient and reasonable basis for a Restraining Order is met before it is meted under these powers.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Would this also possibly include well-meaning ground-up initiatives, registered community-based organisations or registered charities that seek to support specific racial groups as part of each community's efforts to also uplift their own?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Would this be a rather wide and encompassing definition that needs better scoping and specificity for the purposes of this Bill, and instead of encouraging ground-up community efforts, could this instead raise concerns and prevent people from stepping forward to contribute more fervently towards building the social, economic, educational, linguistic and cultural interests of particular aspects of a race or community, which is really the rich diversity we want to preserve and encourage in Singapore, and also allow to flourish.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, also echoing what some hon Members have mentioned earlier, in part six offences relating to race, under offence of inciting enmity against persons distinguished by race and so on, in clause 40, I wonder if this, in any way, could affect our arts community in their good work today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We agree, and I am sure with a resounding consensus in this House, that we are firmly and flatly against any form of intentional incitement of ill will and hostility across racial lines.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This, I have also outlined, in rather unequivocal terms, in the Malay portion of my speech earlier.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate, however, that the arts is and can be a powerful medium for expression of differing and diverse views, and sometimes emotive opinions, serving as a vehicle for social commentary, political critique, personal reflection and advocacy.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, the arts asks inconvenient questions, presses on hot button issues and could upset people.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In light of how clause 40 is worded, could the Ministry reassure the arts community and its enthusiasts, especially those in the visual, literary and performing art forms, that even on sensitive topics relating to race, where sometimes, there could be questions or challenges about racial stereotypes and identities, these would still be permitted with within the remit of artistic licence and what is considered reasonable.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: My view is that some latitude should be given for the relevant art forms to express views, to ask the hard questions, to challenge narratives and to inspire change.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, when done well and tastefully, society would be more cohesive, more thoughtful and more reflective in the longer term, even though it could stir uncomfortable emotions and disdain in the short term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Such a situation is, however, not something to be taken for granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong in 2017, and I quote: "there is nothing natural about where we are – multiracial, multi-religious, tolerant and progressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We made it happen and we have got to protect it, nurture it, preserve it and never break it." Senior Minister Lee's comments were true then and remain true today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Bill could contain a provision that stipulates that Restraining Orders can only be made once all other options have been exhausted and that the conditions of the restraining order are: directly proportional to the behaviour of concern; the least intrusive or restrictive remedy available to achieve the desired outcome and clearly aimed at modifying behaviour of concern, and are not used to punish people Mr Speaker, my second issue relates to community education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In an ideal world, this Bill would be unnecessary and Singaporeans would not engage, certainly not deliberately, in any act that "causes feelings of enmity, hatred, ill will, or hostility between different races", or "incites, instigates or encourages a person" to do the same.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am particularly interested to hear about any such programmes that have been co-designed by children and young people from different cultural, racial and religious groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to that, it is important that in any society people can safely raise or ask legitimate and genuine topics or questions about race and religion, yet to do so in a sensitive and constructive manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that in appropriately curtailing actions or discussions that are racially offensive or insensitive, we do not inadvertently curtail curious conversation or dialogue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly important for children and young people who can be naturally inquisitive about difference, and who need to be provided safe opportunities to ask about race and religion, and to learn about diversity, tolerance and inclusion. : Mr Speaker, related to the above, is the issue of new citizens, PRs and other foreigners living in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that we assist all Singaporeans, including those new to our country, to not engage in any behaviour that may inadvertently offend or distress others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Council is an extension of the current Presidential Council for Religious Harmony and that it is to have a range of functions related to racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I support the establishment of such a Council and would like to know what mechanisms are in place to ensure that membership of the Council is representative of the diverse Singapore community, and that individual members have the necessary expertise and experience to undertake their role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to know how the Council intends to seek the views and opinions of the Singaporean community when making decisions, including the views and opinions of children and young people, women, foreign workers and other at-risk groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to know whether it is intended that any of the CRIs will formally incorporate the principles and practices of restorative justice, a model of community healing that is particularly relevant to racial harmony.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Bill could contain a provision that stipulates that foreign influence Restraining Orders, just like Restraining Orders in general, can only be made once all other options have been exhausted and that the conditions of the restraining order are directly proportional to the issue of concern; the least intrusive or restrictive remedy available to achieve the desired outcome and clearly aimed at modifying behaviour of concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Entities may not always be aware of their obligations regarding foreign influence or may be engaging in behaviour without intent and these entities should be alerted and supported as early in the process as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A substantial proportion of racially offensive or inappropriate material is disseminated online, including from overseas or anonymous sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The harm can be worse for those who experience discrimination on several fronts, such as race, gender, age, religion and disability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Supporting victims of racism is a responsibility we all share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This means standing up against negative stereotypes, intervening in instances of interpersonal racism and advocating for fair practices in our institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We must create safe spaces where victims feel heard, validated and supported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Racism can be individual or personal or it can be systemic or structural.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of the form it takes, we all have a role to play to be vigilant in our own behaviour and the behaviour of others and to speak up if something is not right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot and should not, only rely on others to do something, or on laws or guidelines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is about taking personal responsibility and working collectively to stamp out racism wherever and whenever it occurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can assist make Singapore a place where everyone, regardless of their race, feels safe, welcome and respected.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As someone of mixed race parentage, I recall my late mother telling me about how, as a Chinese lady dating an Indian man in the 1960s in Singapore, there were more than a few occasions where they were subject to some rather unkind comments and there were even places in Singapore that she and my father could not go to as a mixed race couple because of a very real threat of physical violence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My mother also shared the story of how, as a teenage girl, she had to go to the hospital to identify the body of a minority race friend who had been killed when he was innocently swept up in a racially-charged act of violence and I can still recall the deep emotion in her voice as she told me this story, with a somber reminder of how "we should never, ever take racial harmony in Singapore for granted." It is with these words in mind that I rise in full support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I applaud the Government’s position, Mr Speaker, that criminal prosecution is not the first recourse and sole remedy to racial incidents, considering that a good number of such incidents were not committed with the intent to injure anyone’s feelings, but largely arising from lack of cultural understanding and sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An effective CRI must be supported by a structured set of interventions that are evidence-based so that it can achieve its intent to help those who are undergoing the intervention to understand the impact of his or her conduct, reconcile and make amends within the community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can shed light on how such interventions are developed and delivered, and would like to ask if the Government will be setting up an expert taskforce to design, implement and oversee the CRIs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask how would the effectiveness of these CRIs be measured so that their efficacy can be assessed?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And with each transgression being different, would the Government be offering targeted interventions so that maximum level of reconciliation can be achieved?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to suggest that we consider using the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) to rehabilitate individuals who are referred to the community remedial initiative.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are present and they have been a key pillar of helping to maintain racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, the remediation process using the IRCCs could be similar to how radicalised individuals are currently being rehabilitated, but at a less severe, stepped-down level within the community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, Mr Speaker, reconciliation is a two-party effort.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it would be fairly legislatively simple to compel registered entities to disclose their source of donations, foreign affiliations, if any, and the composition of their governing body, how does the Government intend to compel unincorporated associations to do the same?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
