text: This is under the assumption that these associations are informal entities and are loose gatherings of like-minded individuals that the Government does not necessarily have oversight of or has much information on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I hope the Government can shed more light on how it plans to exercise supervision over these entities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these nationality-based restrictions may, in theory, safeguard designated entities from foreign influences, such arrangements might not provide sufficient guardrails.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the leadership team of a designated entity could comprise mainly newly naturalised Singaporeans or PRs who may still have personal historical linkages to foreign entities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I believe that we should not – and I say it again – we should not unfairly shine the spotlight on newly naturalised Singaporeans or PRs, it is empirically difficult for the Government to police personal affiliations of individuals, both local born and naturalised alike.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I would like to suggest an additional safeguard that I hope that the Government can consider the implementation of a two-tier structure for designated entities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the last Committee of Supply debate for MHA, I asked for an update on this proposed Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill, and I am happy to see this well thought through and comprehensive Bill before us today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most important aspect of racial harmony is the day-to-day actions each of us takes to build bridges with people of different races.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government has policies that nudge us in this direction, including ethnic quotas for public housing and the requirement for minority representation for contesting in GRCs for our elections.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most of us have close friends of all races and understand the customs and traditions of one another.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, notwithstanding the racial harmony we generally enjoy in Singapore, there remain issues beneath the surface and we cannot take our harmony for granted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, legislation remains a necessary tool to promote and maintain racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have had offences in relation to racial harmony in the Penal Code in the old sections 298 and 298A, and the substance of these offences remain in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, the new language adds clarity by specifying the actual actions that constitute the offence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The offences in section 298A of promoting enmity between races and engaging in acts prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony remain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While prosecutions under these sections are not common, I think they send an important signal on what is unacceptable conduct.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also three important new tools this Bill provide MHA more powers to better calibrate and deal with the potential threats to racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This seems to be an intermediate step that allows swift action without the need to prosecute the wrongdoer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note that these orders will be subject to review by the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony and the President, which, in my view, is an important check.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A similar regime exists in relation to religious harmony under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and I think it is sensible for those principles to apply here as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This gives MHA a more calibrated set of tools so that less serious offenders may be given a chance to mend their ways and avoid a criminal conviction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will be interested to know how MHA intends to apply these measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think MHA will probably need to develop a set of interventions and procedures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will also probably be a need to have skilled professionals to both help raise awareness and encourage amity between the offender and the community.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The aim of this provision seems to go beyond a simple Corrective Work Order type regime, and building bridges and amity is much more difficult than dishing out punishment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I look forward to seeing how MHA will apply these powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It will also be important to develop some internal guidelines, at least on when this discretion will be exercised, though in my view it would be best to have this as the first port of call for most first-time offenders unless it was a particularly serious offence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I declare that I am involved in a voluntary capacity in a number of race-related charities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am the advisor to the board of trustees of Singapore Indian Development Association, and I am a trustee of the Singapore Indian Education Trust as well as a trustee of the Singapore Indian Fine Arts Society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note from Minister of State Sun's speech that charities have not been listed amongst the entities that MHA intends to designate at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This should be a relief to many of them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a matter of principle though, I believe that while race-based groups play an important role in preserving culture and tradition, it is important for Singapore-based groups to be rooted in our values as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The requirement of a largely Singaporean leadership supports this objective.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also agree that foreign donations should be disclosed, though I think we should also send the message that there is nothing wrong with getting donations from foreigners per se, especially for charitable institutions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many charitable groups may benefit from raising funds from a larger group of donors, including foreigners, and the beneficiaries of these charities are ultimately going to be primarily Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really gratifying to see that there is unanimous agreement on the need for the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some questions, some concerns, and I do note the Workers' Party's position that they will support the Bill but not the Constitution (Amendment) Bill because they have specific concerns about the President having the power to disagree with the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He expressed, as I see it, two main concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He gave examples of CECA, the Palestinian issue and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also said that since this is such an important Bill, it really ought to have been sent to the Select Committee like the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I appreciate his comments, but I think there is some serious misconception on what this Bill does or what it is intended to cover.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would refer Members to Annex 1 and the press release of MHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hopefully, that will help in responding to Mr Giam's comments, Ms Poa's comments and also some of the others who expressed some concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is, in fact, no change in the law." If you look at paragraph 12, on the substantive provisions, because paragraph 11 sets out what is being brought over from the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some updates will be made to align the language and defences under the Bill with the equivalent provisions." So, the changes are that we actually provided for some additional defences and in fact, narrowed one of the provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code and then you look at clauses 39 and 40 of the Bill, they are the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I understand from Mr Giam's speech, he accepts that today, there are no unacceptable constraints on discussing CECA, Palestinian issues and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sections 298 and 298A have been in force for 17 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If no concerns have been expressed until now, I am a slight loss – what is the additional concern with clauses 39 and 40?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Up to today, I am not aware of any concerns expressed in Parliament about sections 298 or 298A of the Penal Code or any suggestion that they should be repealed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Penal Code has been debated a number of times, on various occasions in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point, perhaps, was picked up by Ms Chandradas because she did say yes, the provisions are the same, but since we are coming back to Parliament, perhaps we can re-debate it or debate it anew.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fundamental power, as you would see in clause 8, relates to issuing Restraining Orders; if you look at the provisions, they go back, essentially, to clauses 39 and 40.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think there is a degree of misconception, which then leads to concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the same reason, therefore, the substantive law remains the same with the addition of some processes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, I think you can understand why we do not need a Select Committee, particularly as those additional provisions – Restraining Orders, the Presidential Council, CRI – these are modelled after the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Giam also asked about members of public and can they engage in racial politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The answer is they can continue to do, after this Bill is passed, what they have been doing until now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will just say, have a care on racial politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you get to the line of inciting violence, anything along those lines, which sections 298A and 298 deal with, then you could be transgressing the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would add one more point because this is such a fundamental misconception that we do not want to unduly alarm the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I know sometimes speeches are made with the purpose of the public in mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not suggesting that Mr Giam or anyone else has made such a speech, but it is sometimes tailored for putting out in social media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think all of us agree that we do not want the public to be misled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would suggest that if speeches are put out, which could be misleading on their own, then some care should be taken to give the correct impression of the debate, under the Parliamentary Proceedings Act and the correct impression of the Bill, as clarified by me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum and Mr Louis Ng what measures are in place to address the root causes of racist conduct and support victims of racism and if there are plans to complement measures under the Bill with public campaigns or education efforts promoting racial harmony, and how the public can play a role in safeguarding social cohesion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said a number of times, both in my earlier speech as well as outside this Chamber and in this Chamber on other occasions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members know that that has to be achieved through a multifaceted programme or policies, including public education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I welcome those questions by Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum because it helps us explain this clearly that what the aim of the Bill, just in case members of public think that we are putting in this Bill and relying on it solely to achieve racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is intended to achieve racial harmony but not solely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then, you need a whole lot of other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I referred to in my earlier speech, there are thousands of activities that take place every weekend organised by People's Association (PA), which is a key nation-building agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It makes people come together every weekend and, as a result, then, you interact with each other, you go for each other's events, you celebrate the festivals, week in, week out, throughout the year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is one of the secret sauces that make Singapore successful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why PA has been a key enabler of the success of this country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is one facet; so many other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have talked about the schools being integrated, housing estates being integrated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the legal framework tells you what you cannot do and it helps to set a set of values which are hard-wired, hopefully, into our society over time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the other examples would be the Character and Citizenship Education lessons in schools.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Students are provided a safe space to understand the importance of racial and religious harmony in our multicultural society, and to develop an appreciation of different perspectives and sensitivities around racial and religious issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should note Mr Yip's emphasis on the importance of community participation in building racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a view that is shared by many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Hazel Poa, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Mr Yip and other Members asked how we can ensure that the Restraining Orders for the Bill does not stifle race-related discussions and that the Restraining Orders are not used disproportionately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we can look at the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act for reference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had similar powers for over 30 years, and the powers have never been used.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That gives you an indication of how the Government approaches these powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The important thing is to have the powers, but also to be very, very careful and judicious in how you use them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, there are safeguards in place on the use of the Restraining Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Restraining Orders can only be used by the Minister who has to be publicly accountable, including in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And after the Restraining Order is issued, it has to be sent to the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A person subject to a Restraining Order may make representations to the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony, and that Council must make recommendations to the President whether to confirm, cancel or vary the order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thereafter, the President must consider the recommendation by the Council, along with Cabinet's advice and he can cancel, confirm or vary the Restraining Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, the President must act in accordance with the Cabinet's advice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Neil Parekh, Dr Syed Harun, Ms Chandradas, Ms Poa and Mr Louis Ng asked about the thresholds for issuing Restraining Orders and the safeguards on the issuance of the Restraining Orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling's speech has covered most of these questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, this is necessary in the current day in the context of social media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reference point again is the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore is, I would say, a highly religious society, and if people say that is a subjective opinion, at least, we can say it is quite a religious society, a religious place, and the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act in place for 35 years has not had any curtailing effect on how it has been used.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will come back to this point again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The real point is that we must have the ability to act quickly, decisively, because trust and goodwill, an understanding between our communities, once damaged, can be difficult to restore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Persons issued a Restraining Order will need to comply with it immediately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as Minister of State Sun had mentioned, they may make representations within 14 days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Restraining Order will then be subject to review by the Presidential Council, Cabinet and the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To Ms Poa's question, there is no change in the maximum duration for the Presidential Council to make its recommendation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Extensions of Restraining Orders are also subject to the checks and balances that I had noted above.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Restraining Order cannot be varied when it is extended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Minister wishes to change the terms of an order, he will have to cancel the Restraining Order before issuing a fresh Restraining Order with the new terms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will have to go through the usual review process, including confirmation by the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Poa expressed concerns about the Minister extending an Restraining Order indefinitely to keep a journalist or editor out of their work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is done, it will be an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be an abuse of power to extend the Restraining Order just to keep a person out of work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The extension of Restraining Orders are subject to the same review process and will be considered by the Presidential Council and the President, and if the Minister has no good explanation, he can be overruled; and such an act of extension can also be scrutinised in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need the power to deal with the threats to racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, the Government is voluntarily frame-working in some checks on their power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would say, as was the point made slightly earlier, the best evidence of how these powers are likely to be used is how the Government has used very similar powers under the Maintenance Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But having the legal framework and the power mean that everyone understands, everyone is careful and that, coupled with the whole lot of other policies that I have talked about, has meant that we have not gotten into the problems that others have gotten into.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will give you an example of one case where we did not issue an Restraining Order, but having those powers was useful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the way we do things in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one needs to feel ashamed and we did not need to resort to issuing an order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he had disagreed, we may have had to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the fact that we had the power, I think helped.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Parekh also asked about the role of the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will not have powers to issue binding guidelines or rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ng asked why do we have a combined council, instead of two different councils, one for race and one for religion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of people who are upstanding lay people, community leaders, religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rather than having two, it seemed to us it made sense, race and religion, the issues sometimes overlap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, quite frequently, they may overlap, and it is not always straightforward to disentangle the two.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Have good people, have one composite council, makes much more sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We thought that it was more effective, more efficient, helps better consultation and discussions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had initially started off thinking that we may need two and after a lot of discussions we decided we will have one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Razwana Begum, as well as Mr Louis Ng and Ms Chandradas asked about further details on the composition of the council and its procedures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Ms Sun has mentioned, appointments to the council must seek to ensure that its representatives from the major racial and religious communities in Singapore, and those who have distinguished themselves in public service or community relations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Presidential Council for Minority Rights will advise on the appointments to this Council and members of the arts community who fulfil these criteria can be appointed to the Council.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want to say members of this community, or such other community would be appointed, but there is no automatic veto against the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 33(5) of the Bill, empowers the Council to invite any person to attend before the Council and to examine the person orally, and consider that in the context of its deliberations on a Restraining Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond this, as the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony is intended to be an independent body, it will be allowed to regulate its own procedures within the framework of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given the inherently sensitive nature of the Council's discussions and so as to provide a forum for its members to express themselves freely, the Bill provides for the proceedings of the Council to be private and secret, unless its public disclosure is expressly authorised by the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim expressed concerns about the role of the elected President under this Bill, in making decisions on matters related to race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have touched on this very briefly earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I understand it, Ms Lim and the Workers' Party are not objecting to the Restraining Order regime, but what she does not agree with is the Presidential review of the Restraining Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Workers' Party's view is that the Parliament and the public checks on the Minister are adequate and there should not be an additional layer of checks through the Presidential Council and the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is similar to the model we have adopted in other legislation, like the Internal Security Act and Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, that does not prevent Parliament from asking questions of the Minister or holding him accountable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in all of this, this is a question of judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ultimately, whether the system works really depends on the integrity of the people involved – all the way – the Minister, the Council, the President, Parliament and everywhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony, by bringing in senior leaders in the religious and lay community, can provide an additional rigour to the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can tell Members, because Ms Lim sort of alluded to it, we have certainly not put these provisions in, in the belief that the Presidential Council for Racial and Religious Harmony and the President will never disagree with the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will be an untenable supposition if that was a supposition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are building frameworks and institutions which we hope will see Singapore through over a long period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is all part of the institution building that has been going on over the last 60 years or so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can now turn to some comments that Ms Hazel Poa made, I can see that she is concerned in parts and, again, I think, Ms Poa's comments arose from not realising what is current law is and that the key charging provisions are substantially the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Ms Poa will see, when she quoted in her speech from the Bill, and she said: while this Bill borrows the language found in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, the phrase and act that causes feelings of enmity, hatred, ill will or hostility between different races in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will see that that is pretty much what that is in section 298A today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are additional provisions, as I mentioned earlier, relating to the Restraining Orders, the CRI.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The charging provision, as it were, remains substantially the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the specific examples that she has given on Mr Shaik Amar, I do not recall precisely what the facts were relating to Mr Shaik Amar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I know he said something about EIP and there was a POFMA Order issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not believe he was charged and my recollection is I do not remember anything he said as crossing the criminal threshold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he did not cross the criminal threshold then, he would not cross the criminal threshold now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On "Free Palestine Now!", I do not believe that this was considered an offence at that time it was said and I also do not believe that clauses 39, 40 will be triggered now if it is put into an Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Israel-Hamas, which is another example in that context – "Free Palestine Now" – I have spoken about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for social media comments that are being posted and so on, it depends.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if the law is breached, whether it makes sense for it to be pursued and those are matters where AGC will have to come in to. "From river to sea" is another point that Ms Poa made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She asked if that would be an offence now and whether a Restraining Order can be issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She did note that the Police said that it may have been an offence; the Police statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I want to be careful what I say about this, because the Police statement was clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is up to the Police to decide what they will do about a potential offence that has been disclosed, where they have gone out in public and said they think that there may be a potential offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want to go beyond that, but if they are able to investigate, they wish to investigate because they think there was an offence, after this Bill comes into law, if Parliament passes it, they will be able to do the same now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether a Restraining Order should be issued, depends on clause 8 and whether clause 8 is triggered, and that, in turn, depends on the actual facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then the point about umbrellas with watermelons and wearing the Palestinian motif headgear, and so on, they were not offences per se under sections 298 or 298A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They would not be offences per se now and I would suggest, therefore, a careful understanding of the provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, there is a serious risk that the public may be misled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This issue of umbrellas and cause-related gatherings, you got to differentiate between what this Bill does – clauses 39, 40, taken from 298 and 298A – with gathering in protected places or in being in breach of the Public Order Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you gather in some places in front of Parliament, in front of Istana, gathered at protected places, then you may be committing an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not because you are carrying an umbrella with some motifs or you are wearing a particular headgear, but because you are doing something in a protected place that the law prohibits you from doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that the underlying expression of your ideas about Palestine are in themselves an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, again with Ms Poa, I would say I understand the concerns, but please read the provisions carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum and Mr Louis Ng asked what measures are in place to address the root causes of racist conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do we support victims of racism and whether there are plans to complement measures under the Bill to support this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained that in quite considerable detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Mark Lee, Mr Zhulkarnain, Mr Neil Parekh and Dr Syed Harun asked which entities would be designated under this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 15 of the Bill describes what a race-based entity is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The definition has been kept somewhat broad because of the nature of malicious foreign influence, which can exploit a wide range of entities to further their own agenda and undermine our racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as Minister of State Sun Xueling has mentioned, we intend to designate entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will take a very practical and measured approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No other entities will be designated for now, though we will not preclude designating them in the future, as the threat environment evolves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of public who come across any activity which they consider suspicious, or linked to foreign interference, can let the Internal Security Department know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee asked if there are avenues to appeal against the designations and if there would be flexibility in the leadership requirements imposed on designated entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As part of their representations, the entity can explain why they think they should not be designated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The competent authority will take these representations into account when making the final decision on designation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can also apply, the entities, to the competent authority to have their designations cancelled instead of being varied if there is a material change in the circumstances that no longer warrants designation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Mark Lee, Mr Neil Parekh and Dr Syed Harun asked about the extent of foreign influence that exists in clan and business associations and if the foreign influence safeguards under the Bill would deter or act as a deterrence from individuals participating in race-based activities, would they stifle the activities?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there were some points made about the importance of Singaporeans and our associations and entities being able to interact with foreigners and foreign entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For a start, let me make this clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We agree entirely that Singapore must remain open.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must be able to reach out to the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, we have to, for our success.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at one of the underlying themes of speeches by various government leaders over the last 60 years, it is about being open, interacting with the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Economically, we will be finished if we do not interact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to get ideas from outside and then we need to interact and adapt the ideas that work for us to our own situations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In every way, Singapore survives by relying on being nimble and that means understanding the world and moving ahead or trying to keep a step ahead of any others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That can only happen if you form international partnerships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, yes, I do not think there is any difference in viewpoints or disagreement that we need the world and we need to interact with the world and we need to form partnerships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The real issue is, with the good comes sometimes the bad and clan associations, partnerships and so on can potentially be vectors of influence from countries that want to influence our politics in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are certainly some reasons to be concerned and you see evidence all over the world where there are such vectors of influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had FICA which was passed in this Parliament where Members of Parliament were subjected to various requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that all of you are today vectors of influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we see that countries use legislators, Members of Parliament, Ministers sometimes for pushing their own interests overseas and we are taking precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, we have identified this sector and we are taking the precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It simply means that the entities or the entity has engaged in activities that relate to race, which sometimes is its raison d'etre and we all recognise that these entities are important for Singapore and they play a very a constructive role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They help build social bonds, they preserve our traditions and cultures, they strengthen business networks amongst the many other good things they do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at the same time, the nature of their activities makes them more susceptible to foreign influence and that foreign influence is malicious then it can damage us so we need to take some precautions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, all religious groups are subject to such safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for this Bill, the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill, given that race-based entities are a more diverse group compared to religious groups, our approach has been to have the safeguards apply only to a subset of designated entities and we believe that is enough to meet our policy intent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Designated entities can continue to engage their counterparts overseas including in the pursuit of cultural or commercial goals and, as I said, designation in itself does not impute that they are guilty of any misconduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Designated entities will be subject to transparency requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there are no prohibitions or implications on their activities in the first instance and we have engaged many of these race-based entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They understood and accepted the need for these safeguards to mitigate foreign influence risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ultimately, our intent is to safeguard Singapore from malicious foreign influence, not to curtail any legitimate exchanges, business deals or trade promotion activities conducted by our clan or business associations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Mr Lee, Mr Tan and Mr Parekh asked what would be considered foreign donations and foreign affiliations under the Bill and how the Government would help entities to comply with the foreign influence safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Similar to when such safeguards were introduced under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, my Ministry will provide an information kit in due course to guide designated entities in fulfilling the requirements and will provide reasonable time for the entities to adjust to these changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Yip and Mr Zhulkarnain asked how the Bill interacts with FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: FICA is designed to apply when the risk is specific or when the risk is quite high because of the political nature of the entity or the individual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whereas this Bill is intended to cover broad categories of race-based entities that are assessed to be susceptible to malicious foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David and Mr Yip asked about the effectiveness of the foreign influence safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look, the baseline safeguards that are in the Bill will not be able to completely eliminate the risk of foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where we uncover specific risks or heightened risks, we will have to consider issuing Restraining Orders to impose additional measures against foreign influence or go to FICA and consider the levers under FICA to deal with the risks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That could include imposing additional restrictions on leadership, requiring all the office bearers to be Singapore Citizens if we are of the view that the designated entities have a higher risk of foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is therefore the two-tier approach: baseline safeguards and then additional orders if there are higher risks, which is the two-tier approach suggested by Mr David.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked what mechanisms are in place to allow the Ministry to take down racially problematic materials that are hosted online domestically or internationally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Bearing in mind, we do not control the platforms and there is a limit to what we can do internationally, even within Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Bill complements the levers available under these other legislation and we have some powers to deal with the content that seeks to undermine racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition to Restraining Orders that can be issued to take down such content, offences under the Bill are provided extra-territorial effect, So, that allows us to address persons in other jurisdictions who act in a manner prejudicial to racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Syed Harun and Ms Chandradas asked if offences under the Bill will have an impact on the arts community and their work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I go back to the point I made in response to Mr Giam and Ms Poa: if they have no concern today on what they are doing, then they should have no concerns about what they will be doing tomorrow or the day after the Bill becomes an Act and comes into force because the provisions are substantively similar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Chandradas asked about the defences under the Bill and when they will apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can go back to the earlier point, again I would say in our speeches and in the points we make, we have to be careful not to frighten one community or another community as to what the Bill covers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think an accurate understanding of the Bill, both within the Chamber and outside the Chamber, is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, the Bill has new provisions: the Restraining Order, other levers beyond prosecution and the Presidential Council.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are all additional measures; whereas previously, what we could do was either charge or not charge the person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in terms of what they can do, the two provisions – sections 298 and 298A – they are essentially carried over and there are two separate debates, whether that is too restrictive, which is the point Ms Chandradas alluded to briefly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the question here is whether we can proceed with the Bill, which is in the terms that I have described.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Chandradas asked about the defences under the Bill and when they will apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The defences are scoped to provide space for honest and fair discussions about race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The defences will not apply for the offences of urging violence on the grounds of race, against racial group or its members and I do not think anyone here would suggest that we go that far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I took some trouble in my opening speech to draw the distinction between the way we approach this and how many other countries approach it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When it crosses the line into hate speech or speech that advocates violence, we say no.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, regardless of which community, whether it is defined by race or defined by some other characteristic, we say "No, you cannot advocate violence".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Yip, Mr Zhulkarnain, Mr Parekh, Mr David, Assoc Prof Razwana, Mr Giam and Mr Vikram Nair asked for more details about the CRI.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their questions have mostly been addressed in my earlier speech, and I have also noted Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr David's suggestions for the programme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To briefly recap, the programme is similar to the CRI in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An example of a CRI could be requiring the alleged offender to go and make amends with the aggrieved community that he has in some way attacked and is in breach of the provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if it is properly structured, it can actually lead to better outcomes than charging such a person and imposing a fine or sending him or her to jail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could lead to a better understanding, better appreciation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hopefully, both sides will go away feeling better about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Mr David is right that the content of each programme offered would have to be customised to some extent, depending on the specifics of the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And individuals with entrenched racist views, and there will be some, they cannot be forced to change their views or express genuine remorse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That said, I think it is good that CRI is offered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really gives the alleged offender an opportunity to learn the mistake of his actions, his racist conduct and help soothe communal tensions and repair the disrupted ties between the communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before I conclude, Sir, I would like to address some of the other suggestions made by Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Assoc Prof Razwana asked how we can better integrate foreigners and new citizens into Singapore society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a large topic and it is outside the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will just make the point that the Government agrees that this should be a priority and the point has been addressed elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the very foundation upon which Singapore's success and identity are built.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore is an outlier when compared to other multiracial countries in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are racially diverse, yet we live in harmony and in a high-density city-state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is, as I said, not the natural state of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is sustained through a suite of policies, laws, programmes and, more fundamentally, by Singaporeans' shared commitment to racial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill reflects our collective resolve to cherish and protect this harmony, so that future generations of Singaporeans will continue to enjoy peace and progress for years to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I ask Members for their clarifications, Leader, do you want to move the Exempted Business Motion?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now have clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: One is on my own speech and the second is a clarification on the Government's position.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First of all, earlier in the Minister's round-up, he quoted me saying, because I mentioned that the Government is accountable for decisions on Restraining Orders through Parliament and in that way, accountable to Singaporeans through this forum that these are adequate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I was making that as a comparison in questioning the wisdom of making the EP the final arbiter of whether Restraining Orders are appropriate under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification I have is for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Again, it relates to the EP being designated as the final arbiter in such matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of course, under the scheme, there are other decisions, if we look at the decisions that the EP has been emplaced with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Decisions like whether to allow drawdown of past Reserves, decisions like whether to concur with Public Service appointments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is he not concerned that this scheme here will risk the EP being polarised along racial lines and it is actually really not a road we want to go down?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can summarise the point made by Ms Lim, where the EP disagrees with the Government or the Minister, he becomes the final arbiter, and such a confrontation detracts from the President's normal role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that we have a number of places in the Constitution, situations where the President has such a role – Reserves, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But here, we are dealing with race and is that not a cause for concern?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other countries – first of all, I do not know of other countries which do this sort of thing – but the usual route is having the courts to have a judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The courts sitting in there, dealing with, perhaps, a highly emotive issue and the matter being made a cause célèbre.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In my experience, that usually makes things much worse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, we deliberately went down this route – that we will have Restraining Orders and then, have the final check through a Council and a President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know if the Workers' Party objected to the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act with those provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Internal Security Act, too, we have a similar provision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the President disagrees with the Minister, it is a matter of confrontation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not the most pleasant of things, but as I said, you have to design these laws with a view to build up institutions for the benefit of Singapore as a whole, predicting a time when most of us may not be around, how does it serve Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a curious reversal of roles, because I am here arguing for an extra layer of check on the Government, whereas Ms Lim is saying, why are we having this additional layer because it brings the President into the fray.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if you have outstanding people in the Presidential Council and they are advising the President – senior community leaders and leaders of religious groups, together in their collective wisdom, they think that the Government's Restraining Order lacks substance and they advise the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the President himself is elected by the people and in that sense, he has a mandate, he is accountable to the people himself while the Minister continues to be accountable in Parliament and, of course, to the judgement of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We take the view that if there is such a confrontation, then what it means is a group of outstanding people, the Presidential Council and a person who was directly elected by the people of Singapore, the President, takes a view which is different from the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we think that that should be given some value.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think to suggest that that should be completely ignored, they should not be given that power – I can see where Ms Lim comes from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are people who can argue that – that it should only be the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think the balance here comes down in favour of having this additional check and letting the Minister understand that he has to have a care in how these powers are exercised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have power, you try and build in a framework that provides for careful and prudent exercise of that power, but all the time, also remembering that we are a small boat in an ocean and we do need power given to the Government, subject to suitable checks, to move fast and move quick.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you have too many checks and balances, nothing gets done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you have no checks and balances, sometimes, you can go very wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are trying to find a balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the best answer I can give.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her earlier point is a clarification of what she had earlier said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I understand the point and I think I do not need to repeat myself.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This power that is given to the EP is actually not inside FICA, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not a legal expert, but I want to clarify with the Minister on this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure, Sir, what the clarification is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Member wants to ask me about FICA, I suggest he puts in a question to that effect.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I think it is a relevant question, Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I want to know is, under FICA, the EP does not have the power to veto the Minister's decision, right?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a number of pieces of legislation where the EP does not have the power to veto the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the Minister's reply at that time was yes, the President has to act according to the recommendation of the Cabinet.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The Minister has said that the provisions in the new Bill is largely similar to current provisions, but I think there is a big difference in clause 8.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Most of my clarifications were with respect to the Restraining Order, which is in clause 8.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Is the Minister saying that the Minister, in making a decision under clause 8, will be using largely the same procedure as the judges?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Because when the Courts make the decision, they are usually bound by legal precedence and there is quite a lot of research involved and it takes time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Since the purpose of clause 8 is for speed, I do not see how that can be possible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: That is why we are trying to find out what is this alternative system that the Minister will be using to make his decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC comes in – that is, if it is believed that an offence has been committed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to charge the person and you have to prove the case in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Either you charge or you do not charge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill, in terms of the offences, clauses 39 and 40, take that approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it ports over sections 298 and 298A, and I made that clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that responds to a number of questions Ms Poa had asked about whether something will or will not be an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Mr Shaik Amar's words, I think, she asked if they would be an offence today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was, for example, "from the river to the sea", and I quote, "can lead to racial tensions and maybe an offence under section 298A of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also distinguished between, for example, you carry umbrellas with watermelon motifs or the Palestinian headgear motif, there might be a misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you do that in front of the Istana or if you come to Parliament and do it, or in some other restricted place like the State Courts, you are not being charged because of carrying around a watermelon motif, but because you are breaching the protected places Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some places are gazetted, a certain conduct is prohibited and whether or not you are carrying a watermelon motif umbrella, you will be charged if you are engaged in activities that are prohibited.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you are not being charged for breaching sections 298 or 298A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you engage in conduct, for example, "from the river to the sea", you can see the Police statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police statement was that it was potentially an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said if it was an offence then, it may be an offence now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not want to go beyond that because Police have issued a statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond being a Bill that consolidates provisions, there are parts which are added.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, there are five aspects to this Bill, one of which is the porting over.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a decision by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is an add-on to the underlying provisions, and the Minister has to be satisfied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the earlier discussion with Ms Lim related to the Minister's decision whether it should be final, subject only to scrutiny by Parliament or it should be subject to the safeguards of a veto by the President, if Cabinet takes one view and the Presidential Council takes a different view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not see that that adds an additional layer of substantially restricting free speech or speech on these issues, because the underlying factors that need to be satisfied are similar to what is required under sections 298 and 298A, albeit the decision is made by the Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I do understand the Minister's explanation with regard to clause 39 and clause 40.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My main query is on clause 8 – basically, how the Minister makes his decision.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As he has pointed out, and this is the Minister making the decision instead of the Courts, the Courts have their own system in the decision-making.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, what I am trying to establish is what is the system that the Minister will be using?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And will they be bound by legal precedence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, the Minister will make a decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it will have to be a process that is swift and fast because of the nature of social media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at the same time, Members will note that there are procedures for appeals and for the appeals to be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may recall that FICA would require the Government to act often on intelligence, on foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And often that information is not something that we can share with third parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at FICA foreign influence countermeasures, we talked about different aspects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let us take something that has happened internationally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Country A gives some money to a politician in Country B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do it covertly and they do it for the purpose of influencing the parliamentarians, journalists and others in such situations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I am on record as saying that many countries do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us not target just one country or another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there is record of us having been victims and there are other situations where we know that attempts have been made a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The idea that we can have something similar to a Presidential Council, comprising 15 to 20 people who will have access to the most classified of information, which potentially destroys our sources of information, sources of intelligence, in order to counter such influence – I cannot even begin to imagine or think that we will be doing that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there, it has to be kept to a very small group intentionally because of national interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the context of someone talking about race, there is nothing particularly related to intelligence because it is public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person has said what he has said and now, it is a question of assessment as to whether something ought to be done about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I did not see any particular issue with taking it through this route and having someone potentially review a decision that I or someone else in my position might make.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Could the Minister address my question on how the defence at clause 40(6) will be interpreted?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Is it something that is meant to be interpreted narrowly or will it be considered broadly with regard to the full context of the situation at hand that is being examined?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: So, specifically, if we have an artwork here that is the subject of consideration, will we consider things like the artist's intention as well as the work that is the subject of the consideration?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I trouble Ms Chandradas to tell me which clause she was referring to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 46, it is about the composition of offences by the competent authority?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Clause 40(6), my apologies, where we have to look at the matters of good faith.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, look, I mean, it goes back to the factors that make up the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We look at the issues of feelings of enmity, hatred, ill will, hostility, contempt, ridicule for any race, insult, vilify, denigrate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, we are seeking to give a defence in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That can be taken into account in considering the totality of the situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is there any particular concern about the way it is structured?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: I think, if the Minister will recall, I referred to the example of an artist.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: The example that I talked about was the artist, Lee Wen, in his performance and his works, "The Journey of the Yellow Man".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: So, with this work, he is basically addressing racial stereotypes and it is with a view to prompting audiences to think about the issues.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: So, if we actually look at the work, I do not think we can see a clear message there to bring about a removal of the matters that he is addressing.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: But if you consider the artist's intention in the work that he is producing, you will see that perhaps a different conclusion could be reached.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know this particular work, so I do not want to comment without knowing the details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you frame it as his intention, in the first place, was to educate and not to bring about enmity and ill will, and if that is believed, one has got to look at the nature of the work, what a reasonable person would think, what was his own intention in doing it; and there are a range of possibilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is to say, yes, it is offensive, but we think that this was the reason why he did it, and maybe, we give him a warning to not do it again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or accept in good faith that actually, this might help in the overall maintenance of racial harmony because of the nature of the work.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not see any more hands raised.      .
